## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{100}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}

::: {.content-visible unless-format="pdf"}

![](images/svg/margin_stack.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Physical AI Systems Stack"}

*Physical AI stack focus for this chapter.*

_Why must a moving machine keep checking its commands when its learned model stops responding?_

A learned model can pause for a fraction of a second while it interprets a scene, but the machine carrying it keeps moving, and a loaded base covers tens of centimeters in that pause. Every delay between a decision and the current it becomes is therefore paid in clearance. A general-purpose computer hides such delays behind queues, retries, and priorities. A moving machine cannot, because a command that arrives late acts on a body that has already moved, and a check that waits on the model it checks protects nothing once that model stalls. Treating timing and communication as implementation details produces machines whose safeguards share a processor, a supply rail, or a memory bus with the model they guard, and so fail together with it. A machine that acts on learned decisions therefore needs a timed path between proposal and actuator whose delays are bounded, whose checks never wait on the proposer, and whose grant of authority to each proposal expires on its own. At the causal boundary, time granted to a proposal becomes motion that software cannot recall.

{{< pagebreak >}}

- Evaluate mailbox exchanges for bounded reads, complete payloads, and proposal freshness when the writer stalls
- Size a chunk lease between the renewal floor and the pre-brake ceiling, and explain why a host heartbeat cannot renew it
- Distinguish measured latency percentiles from response-time bounds that include computation, blocking, and interference
- Compare position, velocity, torque, and impedance commands by what each leaves the permission path to check
- Evaluate interface timing violations using handoff records that distinguish allocated budgets, supporting evidence, and unresolved bounds

## The Multi-Rate Bridge {#sec-nervous-multi-rate-bridge}

The running machine joins two computational regimes that run on clocks roughly three orders of magnitude apart. A deep neural network processes camera frames into action proposals over tens to hundreds of milliseconds, with latency that fluctuates from frame to frame. An electric motor drive, by contrast, regulates winding current every few tens of microseconds, in a loop that can never pause because the mass it moves keeps its momentum whether or not a new command arrives. The architectural layer between them, the machine's **Nervous System**\index{Nervous system!architecture}, routes action proposals downward toward the actuators, streams physical telemetry back up, and arbitrates whether any proposal is permitted to move the hardware. Industrial motion control, avionics, and automotive engineering solved similar coordination problems decades ago for classical feedback controllers whose worst-case execution times were statically bounded before deployment [@kopetz2011real]. Learned proposers break those classical assumptions. Their inference latencies have long tails, their software runtimes can stall unexpectedly, and their outputs can fail in ways that cannot be exhaustively enumerated at design time.

This asymmetry sets the chapter's central design question, which @sec-brain left open with two proposers (a chunk policy and an intent model, either of which can stall, miss its deadline, or misjudge the target). The question is how long the physical plant may keep executing the last valid proposal when an inference step stalls or drops a frame. That duration cannot be an arbitrary software timeout or the proposer's own schedule; it must follow from the machine's stopping distance and mechanical limits. @Sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning shows why the timed path to the actuators must remain independent of unbounded interference and stalls from deliberative inference, and states the two-processor split that meets this requirement as a hypothesis the machine's silicon must still confirm under load, while @sec-nervous-cadences derives the rate of each tier from a physical time constant and passes proposals between tiers through a mailbox that never blocks the faster reader. @Sec-nervous-lease-sizing then answers the central question with the *chunk lease*, the bounded interval during which an admitted proposal may keep driving the actuators, priced in the stopping budget, and @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses bounds the computation and the drive network (the *fieldbus*) on which that price depends. Because bounded timing still requires exclusive control of the actuators and survival under host faults, @sec-nervous-actuation-authority and @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation keep the permission path the sole writer of the drives and alive when the proposer fails, @sec-nervous-invariant-checking states the execution contract its checks must meet however fast the proposer runs, and the handoff record of @sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix locates every limit at one of five interfaces, coupling this layer's lease to the stopping distance of the Body and the renewal rate of the Brain.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_pa.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Plan-Act edge."}

*On the sense-plan-act (S·P·A) triad (@sec-appendix-spa), proposals cross from Plan to Act only through the permission path.*
:::

The running machine, the warehouse mobile manipulator, shows the gap concretely. It regulates current through its brushless motor windings thousands of times per second, whereas the vision-language-action (VLA) policies that plan its grasp on a conveyor-belt mug need orders of magnitude longer to evaluate each frame. If motor regulation ever blocks on deliberative reasoning, or contends for shared memory without a bound on its wait, a heavy inference burst can push the control loop past its hard deadline. Moving mass and electromagnetic coils force one conclusion. *The Brain needs time to deliberate, while the Body needs continuous control.*

Coupling these domains across a shared blocking execution path forces the fast loop to inherit the tail latency of the slow one. If the motor control loop stalls waiting for inference or drains an outdated FIFO queue of stale setpoints, the resulting actuation commands arrive at a physical body that has already moved past the target state. Unmanaged transport delay ($\PureTransportDelay$) also injects phase lag directly into the feedback loop, adding $\DelayPhaseLag = \AngularFrequency \PureTransportDelay$ radians at angular frequency $\AngularFrequency$. That lag erodes the loop's phase margin, the extra lag it can absorb before its corrections start to reinforce the motion instead of damping it (made precise in @sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag). The Nervous System must bound these end-to-end transport delays deterministically while ensuring that high-rate local control remains autonomous whenever high-level deliberation stalls.

::: {.column-margin}
<!-- fig-alt hand-types the four periods; MachineTiers guards them (500 ms, 50 ms, 1 ms, 50 us).
     Drawn by generate_margin_figures.py (ch04_cadence_tier_ladder); --check fails on drift. -->
![](images/svg/margin_cadence_tier_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Ladder of four horizontal bars on a log time axis, longest at top: intent 500 milliseconds, chunk 50 milliseconds, tick 1 millisecond, current 50 microseconds."}

*Each tier runs at least ten times faster than the one above it, and none may wait on a slower one.*
:::

To enforce this isolation, the Nervous System splits work across four tiers, separating what each tier controls alongside how often it runs. Each tier runs decoupled from the tiers above it, so fast safety and stabilization loops never wait on slower deliberative tiers:

1. **Actuator current and velocity regulation:** Dedicated motor drives close the inner winding-current and joint-velocity loops locally in hardware. Field-oriented control (FOC)[^fn-foc-motor-drive] aligns the stator voltage vector with the rotor's magnetic flux in every carrier period (the switching period of the drive's pulse-width modulation, or PWM), so the winding produces the commanded torque within a few current-loop samples.
2. **Permission and position supervision:** The deterministic real-time supervisory controller verifies proposal freshness and kinematic limits, sends admitted position setpoints across the fieldbus, checks tracking error against physical safety envelopes, and commands a fail-safe stopping trajectory if proposal authority expires.
3. **Action-chunk policy:** The learned mid-level policy emits a short sequence of future waypoints (an action chunk), giving local controllers a continuous motion segment to track between discrete inference steps.
4. **Intent planning:** Slower vision-language or task-planning models read camera frames and language instructions to set high-level goals, steering the action-chunk policy without directly touching drive setpoints.

[^fn-foc-motor-drive]: **Field-Oriented Control (FOC)**: The drive rotates the three measured phase currents into a frame that turns with the rotor's magnetic field, where torque and flux become two slowly varying currents that ordinary proportional-integral loops can hold. The rotation needs a fresh rotor angle in every carrier period, so the loop cannot wait on anything slower than its own sensors. That is why the current loop runs inside the drive, beside the encoder and the current shunts, and why no proposer, however fast, ever sits inside it. \index{Field-oriented control!drive current loop}

@Sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag gives each tier its rate, while one rule holds all four together and comes first: a stalled or crashed proposer must never block or delay a lower tier's checks. Conventional computing architectures break that rule because they rely on shared processors, unified memory buses, and multi-level caches managed by general-purpose operating systems. In such environments, hardware isolation is weak. When a large deep neural network streams gigabytes of model weights from DRAM across a shared memory fabric, its high-throughput direct memory access (DMA) bursts contend directly with real-time telemetry and control packets. Because hardware bus transactions cannot be preempted by software thread priorities, control packets queue up at the memory controller. A control path that shares an execution environment with machine learning runtimes is also exposed to operating-system jitter, because kernel page faults, garbage collection cycles, driver interrupts, and thermal frequency throttling can each stall execution for tens of milliseconds. Physical stability therefore demands an architecture in which local control loops keep updating the actuators on schedule whatever delays the inference path suffers.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-machine-stall-travel
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BASE TRAVEL DURING ONE PROPOSER INFERENCE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-multi-rate-bridge, the running-machine bullets.
# │ Goal:    Show how far the base moves while each learned proposer computes.
# │ Show:    60 mm in one 40 ms chunk inference, 503 mm in one computed
# │          336 ms intent inference, at the 1.5 m/s drive limit.
# │ How:     Distance = drive limit x inference latency, all from the registry.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class MachineStallTravel:
    """Base travel at the drive limit during one inference of each learned proposer."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    t_chunk = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative (P99, incl. vision)
    t_intent = RM.intent_inference_latency  # category: derived (prefill plus decode, @sec-brain-memory-wall)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_chunk = (v * t_chunk).to(millimeter)
    d_intent = (v * t_intent).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Drive limit drifted: {v}")
    check(abs(t_chunk.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk inference latency drifted: {t_chunk}")
    # 2026-09-28 (M2): intent latency computed, no longer a stipulated 160 ms.
    check(abs(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude - 335.61) < 5e-3, f"Intent inference latency drifted: {t_intent}")
    check(abs(d_chunk.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-6, f"Chunk-inference travel drifted: {d_chunk}")
    check(abs(d_intent.magnitude - 503.41) < 5e-3, f"Intent-inference travel drifted: {d_intent}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_intent_str = fmt_latency(round(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_chunk_str = fmt_length(d_chunk, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_intent_str = fmt_length(round(d_intent.magnitude) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-winding-time-constant
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WINDING TIME CONSTANT OF THE RUNNING MACHINE'S HUB MOTORS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-multi-rate-bridge opening and the current-loop tier
# │          in @sec-nervous-cadences.
# │ Goal:    Use the same registry tau_e that @sec-body-electrical-time-constants
# │          computes, and show where the current-loop bandwidth sits.
# │ Show:    tau_e = 1.885 mH / 0.7 Ohm = 2.7 ms, a plant pole near 59 Hz; the
# │          20 kHz sampling rate caps the closed-loop bandwidth near 2 kHz,
# │          about 34 times above the pole.
# │ How:     tau_e = L/R from RM.drive_unit (ZLTECH ZLLG10ASM800 datasheet);
# │          pole = 1 / (2 pi tau_e); bandwidth cap = f_current / 10.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class WindingTimeConstant:
    """Hub-motor electrical time constant and the current-loop bandwidth window."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    l_line = RM.drive_unit.line_inductance  # category: sourced (line-to-line)
    r_line = RM.drive_unit.line_resistance  # category: sourced (line-to-line)
    f_current = RM.current_loop_rate  # category: chosen (drive current-loop rate)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_e = (l_line / r_line).to(millisecond)
    f_pole = (1 / (2 * math.pi * tau_e)).to(hertz)
    f_bw_cap = (f_current / 10).to(hertz)  # a factor of ten below the sampling rate
    room = (f_bw_cap / f_pole).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_e.magnitude - 2.693) < 1e-3, f"tau_e must match @sec-body (CurrentRise): {tau_e}")
    check(tau_e < RM.chunk_inference_latency, "The winding must settle well inside one chunk inference.")
    check(room > 10, f"The bandwidth window above the pole collapsed: {room:.1f}x")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_e_str = fmt_latency(tau_e, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_pole_str = fmt_frequency(round(f_pole.magnitude) * hertz, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    f_bw_cap_str = fmt_frequency(f_bw_cap.to(kHz), unit=kHz, precision=0)
```

Learned proposers need tens to hundreds of milliseconds to convert raw camera frames into spatial action plans. In the physical domain, an electromagnetic motor winding has an electrical time constant ($\ElectricalTimeConstant = \PhaseInductance/\PhaseResistance$) of a few milliseconds, `{python} WindingTimeConstant.tau_e_str` for the running machine's direct-drive hub motors (@sec-body-electrical-time-constants), while its moving links carry substantial kinetic energy ($\KineticEnergy = \frac{1}{2} \Mass \BodySpeed^2$). Delaying or dropping an actuation command by a fraction of a second can exhaust the clearance before a new inference cycle finishes. On the warehouse robot the mismatch appears in two mechanical domains:

- The base (Class 1) cruises at up to its `{python} MachineStallTravel.v_str` drive limit (illustrative; see the Reader Guide). At this speed, it travels `{python} MachineStallTravel.d_chunk_str` during a single `{python} MachineStallTravel.t_chunk_str` action-chunk inference, and `{python} MachineStallTravel.d_intent_str` across one `{python} MachineStallTravel.t_intent_str` intent-model inference cycle. Unless an independent supervisory process monitors plant telemetry and commands braking, the chassis travels half a meter open-loop before deliberative planning produces an updated command, nearly half the rack-end clear distance on the machine card.
- The arm (Class 2) couples motor rotors to joints through high-ratio gearboxes, reflecting rotor inertia back to the joint output as $\GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia$, the scaling derived in @sec-body-reflected-rotor-inertia. The drives keep closing their own joint loops when the proposer stalls, but they keep tracking the last admitted command. If that command was set for a grasp on a conveyor mug or a turn of a door latch the scene no longer matches, the reflected inertia and the drives together keep pressing the mechanism into the contact, and contact forces escalate rapidly. Whether this interaction breaches structural limits depends on the contact compliance, surface friction, and mechanical response times alongside the reflected inertia.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The intent model's inference latency, priced from its compute-bound prefill and its bandwidth-bound weight sweeps, is established in @sec-brain-memory-wall.
:::

Software discipline, operating system thread priorities, and runtime exception handlers cannot by themselves keep the plant safe. Safety requires an explicit, physically deterministic computing, memory, and communication fabric. That fabric forms the Nervous System of the five-level machine model (@sec-boundary-machine-model), hosting the dedicated permission path so the physical plant retains a measured, feasible response whenever higher-level inference pauses or fails. Its primary design requirement is an interface whose temporal bounds, command authority, and fault responses can be verified directly against the machine's physical safety budget; enforcement algorithms later turn these requirements into per-tick admission decisions, while the mechanisms of this layer fix the contracts those decisions must satisfy.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The per-tick admission decisions that must satisfy these contracts are developed in @sec-enforcement-deterministic-gatekeeper.
:::

## The Independence Requirement and the Two-Processor Hypothesis {#sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning}

When an inference model suffers a transient stall or drops a frame, the robot can safely reject the stale proposal and fall back to local control; when a permission check stalls, however, the delay burns directly through the machine's stopping budget, regardless of whether the processor eventually catches up. The two workloads therefore optimize for different guarantees. A neural chunk policy needs high compute throughput and memory bandwidth to stream motion proposals at its target renewal rate, whereas the permission path needs a strict, provable upper bound on the time required to validate and dispatch each step.

Standard operating-system schedulers decide which ready task executes next, but software priority alone cannot guarantee deterministic timing. Raising a control task's priority reduces processor contention, yet it cannot prevent microarchitectural delays. A sudden page fault suspends execution while the virtual memory subsystem resolves the missing page; lock contention on shared kernel primitives leaves a real-time thread waiting behind uncritical background tasks; and memory requests stall at the arbiter while DMA transfers from a GPU or neural accelerator saturate the system interconnect. Long inference latency tails[^fn-math-inference-latency] therefore threaten closed-loop stability even when average proposal latency remains well within nominal bounds.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-tick-vocabulary
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE PERMISSION TICK AS A PERIODIC REAL-TIME TASK (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning, the real-time vocabulary
# │          paragraph; reused by the RTA example in @sec-nervous-rta-variance.
# │ Goal:    Give period, deadline, WCET, and unloaded execution time on the
# │          machine's own tick so each term is defined on a real quantity.
# │ Show:    period 1 ms; deadline 400 us; declared WCET 250 us; unloaded 135 us.
# │ How:     All from AISLE (the same values @sec-placement uses).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class TickVocabulary:
    """The permission tick's period, deadline, and execution-time terms."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_period = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen (1 kHz permission tick)
    t_deadline = AISLE.enforcer_deadline  # category: chosen
    t_wcet = AISLE.enforcer_wcet  # category: chosen (declared)
    t_unloaded = AISLE.enforcer_unloaded  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_wcet_gap = (t_wcet - t_unloaded).to(microsecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_period.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, f"Tick period drifted: {t_period}")
    check(abs(t_deadline.to(microsecond).magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-9, f"Tick deadline drifted: {t_deadline}")
    check(abs(t_wcet.to(microsecond).magnitude - 250.0) < 1e-9, f"Declared WCET drifted: {t_wcet}")
    check(abs(t_unloaded.to(microsecond).magnitude - 135.0) < 1e-9, f"Unloaded execution drifted: {t_unloaded}")
    check(t_unloaded < t_wcet < t_deadline < t_period, "Unloaded < WCET < deadline < period")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_deadline_str = fmt_latency(t_deadline.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_wcet_str = fmt_latency(t_wcet.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_unloaded_str = fmt_latency(t_unloaded.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_wcet_gap_str = fmt_latency(t_wcet_gap, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
```

Timing guarantees throughout this chapter use the standard terms of real-time scheduling [@buttazzo2011hard; @kopetz2011real], where each term names a part of the permission tick's cycle. The permission tick runs as a periodic task $\RealTimeTaskIndex$ released once every **period**\index{Period (real-time task)} $\TaskPeriod_i$, set here to `{python} TickVocabulary.t_period_str`. Each release is a single job that must finish before its relative **deadline**\index{Deadline!relative} $\TaskRelativeDeadline_i$, measured from the release instant and set here to `{python} TickVocabulary.t_deadline_str`. The deadline is shorter than the period so that each admitted setpoint is ready within the cycle that computed it rather than one tick later, a delay whose cost @sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag prices, and so that the rest of the period stays free for lower-priority work. A deadline is *hard* when a single miss can cause a physical hazard, as on the permission tick, where one late check adds one more millisecond of unchecked motion. The total wall-clock time from task release to job completion is its **response time**\index{Response time} $\WorstCaseResponseTime_i$, and the part of that response time spent running the task's own instructions is bounded above by its **worst-case execution time (WCET)**\index{Worst-case execution time}[^fn-wcet-control-tick] $\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i$.

[^fn-wcet-control-tick]: **Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET)**: A static WCET is a bound proved over every path through the binary and every state the processor's caches and pipeline can be in; analyzers compute it by abstract interpretation of the code against a model of that hardware [@wilhelm2008worst]. Caches, branch predictors, and shared buses make that model either pessimistic or intractable, so a timed path earns a tight bound by avoiding them. The bounded sources listed in @sec-nervous-rta-variance therefore favor tightly coupled memory and fixed pipelines, giving up average speed for a bound that analysis can prove. \index{Worst-case execution time!static analysis}

::: {#dfn-nervous-worst-case-execution-time .callout-definition title="Worst-case execution time"}

***Worst-case execution time***\index{Worst-case execution time!definition}\index{WCET!definition} is the longest time a task can take to run to completion on a given processor, over every admissible input and every state its caches, pipeline, and buses can be in, with no other task competing for the processor.

1.  **Significance**: It is the $\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i$ term of every response bound in this chapter, and every margin above it is sized on it. The permission tick declares `{python} TickVocabulary.t_wcet_str` against an unloaded run of `{python} TickVocabulary.t_unloaded_str`, so the `{python} TickVocabulary.t_wcet_gap_str` between them is a claim that analysis must justify before the `{python} TickVocabulary.t_deadline_str` deadline, and the stopping budget behind it, can rely on the number.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a mean or a high percentile such as $\text{p99}$, which describe the executions a test happened to reach, the WCET covers every admissible path and processor state. A declared WCET is a third quantity, a number the design commits to, which evidence must show is no smaller than the true one.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Recording the largest measured execution time as the WCET. A measured maximum can refute a declared bound but never establish it, because a test campaign reaches only some of the processor states in which the code can run [@wilhelm2008worst].

:::

The rest of the response time is spent waiting rather than running. **Blocking**\index{Blocking time} $\TaskBlockingTime_i$ is the time a task spends waiting for a lower-priority task to release a shared hardware or software resource, whereas **interference**\index{Interference (scheduling)} $\TaskInterferenceTime_i$ is the time taken by higher-priority tasks, kernel interrupts, and exception handlers that preempt the job. Because blocking and interference vary from one release to the next, the exact timing of recurring events shifts from cycle to cycle, a variation called **jitter**\index{Jitter}. Task releases, sensor samples, and job completions each have their own jitter, so a tick released on schedule can still miss its completion deadline if its internal wait times fluctuate. Later, @sec-nervous-rta-variance combines $\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i$, $\TaskBlockingTime_i$, and $\TaskInterferenceTime_i$ into a provable bound on $\WorstCaseResponseTime_i$.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-permission-tick-strip
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LEGO VALUES FOR @fig-04-permission-tick
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: caption of @fig-04-permission-tick and its plotting cell.
# │ Goal:    Compute and guard the values the caption prints, before the
# │          figure div, so the caption can reference them.
# │ How:     See the class docstring; every value from RM / AISLE.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class TickPermissionStrip:
    """One permission tick drawn to scale, with travel per tick."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_period = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: datasheet (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_tick = (v * t_period).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(d_tick.magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Travel per tick drifted: {d_tick}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_tick_str = fmt_length(d_tick, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, precision=1)
```

Placed on one axis, the terms separate an illustrative unloaded observation from the bound the schedule assumes (@fig-04-permission-tick). The unloaded run of `{python} TickVocabulary.t_unloaded_str` is an illustrative observation, not a reported measurement; the `{python} TickVocabulary.t_wcet_gap_str` above it, up to the declared `{python} TickVocabulary.t_wcet_str`, is a claim that WCET analysis must certify; and the slack from there to the `{python} TickVocabulary.t_deadline_str` deadline is all the room left for blocking and interference. Underneath, the base covers `{python} TickPermissionStrip.d_tick_str` during every tick at its `{python} TickPermissionStrip.v_str` drive limit, so each of these microsecond terms is ultimately paid in millimeters.

::: {#fig-04-permission-tick fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**One permission tick**: A job is released at the start of each `{python} TickPermissionStrip.t_period_str` period and must finish by its `{python} TickVocabulary.t_deadline_str` deadline. The unloaded run of `{python} TickVocabulary.t_unloaded_str` is an illustrative observation, not a reported measurement; the declared WCET of `{python} TickVocabulary.t_wcet_str` is the bound the schedule assumes, and the hatched `{python} TickVocabulary.t_wcet_gap_str` between them is what WCET analysis must justify. The slack to the deadline is the budget for blocking and interference. The bottom row counts the base's travel on the same axis, `{python} TickPermissionStrip.d_tick_str` per tick at the `{python} TickPermissionStrip.v_str` drive limit." fig-alt="Timing strip over one millisecond. Top row, illustrative observation: a bar from 0 to 135 microseconds labeled unloaded run. Second row, declared: a solid bar to 135 microseconds, a hatched bar from 135 to 250 microseconds labeled declared WCET 250 microseconds with 115 microseconds to justify, and a dashed outline from 250 to 400 labeled slack 150 microseconds. Vertical lines mark the release at 0, a red dashed deadline at 400 microseconds, and the next release at 1000 microseconds, under a bracket labeled period 1 ms. A travel row below marks 0 to 1.5 millimeters, 1.5 millimeters per tick at 1.5 meters per second."}

from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

strip = viz.permission_tick_strip(AISLE, TickPermissionStrip.v)
strip.lanes[0] = "illustrative observation"
for _s in strip.spans:  # at print width these labels move off the narrow bars
    if _s.label.startswith("slack"):
        _s.label_pos = "below"
    elif _s.label.startswith("unloaded run"):
        _s.label_pos = "above"
        _s.label_dx = 70.0  # clear of the release line
strip.figsize = (6.4, 4.8)  # print scale: the strip's default canvas is 10 in wide
fig, ax, axd = viz.plot_timing_strip(strip)

:::

Blocking introduces an architectural vulnerability that priority schemes alone cannot resolve. In **priority inversion**\index{Priority inversion}, a high-priority task waits for a shared resource held by a low-priority task, while medium-priority tasks that need no shared resource preempt the lock holder and so starve the high-priority task for as long as they run. Only a real-time locking protocol, such as priority inheritance or priority ceiling emulation, can bound that wait. The recurring resets of the 1997 Mars Pathfinder spacecraft are the canonical case of an inversion left unbounded; war story \ref{ws-nervous-1997-mars-pathfinder-priority-inversion} in @sec-nervous-rta-variance traces it once the response-time bound it violated is in hand.

POSIX real-time extensions (such as `SCHED_FIFO` priority scheduling and memory locking via `mlockall()`), real-time Linux kernels (`PREEMPT_RT`), and dual-kernel architectures (such as Xenomai) target specific software sources of delay. Locking physical memory via `mlockall()` eliminates demand paging inside the timed control loop; assigning processor affinity confines threads to specific CPU cores to avoid migration latency and cache thrashing; and priority inheritance elevates a low-priority lock holder's priority whenever a high-priority task requests its mutex. These operating-system mechanisms, however, guarantee determinism only when supported by proper configuration, bounded system calls, and verified timing evidence.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The scheduling, interrupt, and memory mechanisms whose formal contribution enters a response bound are developed in @sec-appendix-systems-timers.
:::

Shared hardware introduces delays that operating-system software priorities cannot control. A control task cannot read an optical encoder buffer while a high-bandwidth peripheral monopolizes a shared PCI Express (PCIe) link or system memory bus. Any physical infrastructure that two processing domains share, whether system memory, power regulation, a thermal path, or a reference oscillator, can delay or silence the permission path without a single software fault. Cataloging those physical couplings and gathering the evidence required to verify their isolation belongs to placement (@sec-placement-two-paths-one-die). The requirement that analysis tests can be stated now. Under any workload the proposer can generate, the permission path must meet its response bound and keep its authority to refuse an unsafe motion. This chapter calls that requirement independence.

[^fn-math-inference-latency]: **Inference Latency Distribution**\index{Inference latency}: The median and $\text{p99}$ alone do not fix the exceedance probability at a given deadline, which must be measured or modeled separately. Tail-model assumptions and exceedance estimates require representative workload data and an account of dependence and uncertainty; @sec-appendix-ml-evt develops these conditions.

The running machine meets the independence requirement by putting the two paths on two processors, a hypothesis it must still test (@fig-04-two-processor-implementation). An application processor runs perception, the 2 Hz intent model, and the 20 Hz chunk policy. A separate safety microcontroller unit (MCU) runs the permission path and alone drives the motors. Between them runs a board link, a serial peripheral interface (SPI) or Controller Area Network with Flexible Data-rate (CAN FD) bus carrying framed packets with cyclic redundancy checks (CRCs) and sequence numbers. The link is treated as a *black channel*, one the endpoints do not trust, so each frame carries its own integrity and timing checks (@sec-nervous-supervisory-timers). The two paths share no processor cores, caches, or memory buses, and the learned proposers on the host have no memory-mapped input/output (MMIO) access to the drive registers. Candidate chunks cross the link into the MCU's own SRAM through a double buffer. A receive DMA transfer fills a private receive buffer, and the receive interrupt copies each checked frame into a single mailbox slot guarded by a sequence lock, or *seqlock*, whose protocol @sec-nervous-mailbox-exchanges develops. A 1 kHz permission tick reads that slot, checks each proposal's freshness, lease, and kinematic limits against measured encoder feedback, and is the only code that can send an admitted setpoint to the drives. The host is an unprivileged client; the microcontroller, with a short and cycle-counted loop, is the part whose worst-case execution time can be bounded.

Physical separation onto separate chips represents one realization. A single system-on-chip can also host both paths, provided that on-chip interconnects, cache partitioning, and memory controllers demonstrate equivalent response bounds and fault containment under stress. Choosing between discrete silicon and partitioned on-chip cores is the central placement trade-off, and until loaded experiments settle it, physical separation remains a foundational design hypothesis. Scheduling both paths on shared processor cores introduces the problem of *mixed-criticality scheduling*\index{Mixed-criticality scheduling!first use}, in which each task carries execution-time bounds of graduated assurance levels and the operating system guarantees each deadline only under the bound its own criticality demands, allowing the proposer to overrun while the permission path executes deterministically [@vestal2007preemptive]. Sharing memory on a single die also demands explicit memory-bandwidth regulation to prevent tensor accelerators from starving real-time safety routines.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Mixed-criticality scheduling, memory-bandwidth regulation, and the other remedies for shared-die contention are developed in @sec-placement-isolation-decisions.
:::

```{python}

A dashed proposal arrow runs from the chunk policy through the link into a double buffer with seqlock, filled by receive DMA in MCU-local SRAM, inside the safety MCU. The buffer feeds a permission tick at 1 kilohertz that checks freshness, lease, and limits. Designating an embedded controller as a *safety microcontroller*\index{Safety microcontroller!definition} claims far more than physical separation on a circuit board. It denotes a device developed, qualified, and assessed under the IEC 61508 functional-safety standard, accompanied by a safety manual specifying its certified integrity level and the operational conditions that support depends on [@iec61508-2-2010]. At the silicon level, a safety MCU integrates specialized hardware redundancy to detect internal faults autonomously: dual processor cores execute in lockstep while a comparator flags divergent execution; error-correcting codes (ECC) protect internal SRAM and flash memories against single-event upsets; a hardware memory protection unit (MPU) confines each task to its assigned memory range; and analog monitors continuously watch the clock and supply voltages. Built-in self-tests run at power-up and periodically during operation to verify internal logic. An external watchdog timer, clocked by its own oscillator and serviced within a strict time window or through challenge-response messages, monitors the core. Because the watchdog relies on an independent clock source, a physical fault that stops the microcontroller's oscillator cannot stall the watchdog, allowing it to detect that silent processor failure and command a qualified out-of-band response. Successful physical containment still depends on the response path, its surviving power, and the actuator premises.

Two different protections meet at this microcontroller, and keeping them apart explains the standards that follow. The chunk lease protects the stopping budget against a proposer that stalls or misbehaves. The rated claim that the machine will not strike a person rests elsewhere, on the independent protective path of @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline (a certified safety scanner wired to the drives, with its own sensing, timing, and power) and on the drives' certified stop functions. Hardware diagnostic features alone do not confer a safety rating on the robot. Under functional safety standards, integrity belongs to a specific safety function, such as revoking actuator authority when a lease expires, rather than to an individual chip. The industrial standard IEC 61508 classifies safety functions by Safety Integrity Level\index{Safety integrity level (IEC 61508)} (SIL 1 through SIL 4), where each numerical increment demands approximately an order-of-magnitude reduction in the allowable rate of dangerous failure [@iec61508]. The machinery standard ISO 13849-1 grades safety functions by Performance Level\index{Performance level (ISO 13849)} (PL a through PL e) [@iso13849part1]. A Performance Level combines four architectural factors: the structural Category (ranging from single-channel architectures using well-tried components in Categories B and 1, through single channels with periodic diagnostic testing in Category 2, to dual-channel redundant designs in Categories 3 and 4 where no single hardware fault defeats safety enforcement); component reliability, quantified as the mean time to dangerous failure; diagnostic coverage\index{Diagnostic coverage}, defining the fraction of dangerous failures detected by internal testing; and physical defenses against common-cause failure\index{Common-cause failure}, where a shared disturbance disables redundant channels simultaneously. The safety microcontroller contributes certified failure rates and diagnostic coverage to this calculation, while the target Performance Level is dictated by the severity and exposure of the physical hazard the safety function must mitigate.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The Performance Level each certified stop and speed function of the running machine must reach is developed in @sec-enforcement-certified-functions.
:::

The physical architecture of the robot makes a deliberate engineering trade-off that functional safety certification must evaluate. Its permission path executes real-time performance tasks, validating trajectory proposals and interpolating admitted waypoints into drive setpoints, alongside the safety function intended for qualification: revoking actuator authority and commanding a safe stop when a chunk lease expires or the host heartbeat falls silent. The algorithmic admission checks themselves carry no formal safety rating, which is why the protective claim stays with the scanner and the drive stop circuits (@sec-enforcement-certified-functions). Standard functional-safety practice keeps complex control algorithms out of the certified safety channel, relying instead on an independent monitoring channel to satisfy Category 3 and Category 4 redundancy requirements. Modern motor drives supply part of that second channel through integrated hardware safety functions such as Safe Stop 1 (SS1), which brakes the motor under drive control and then removes torque.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How Safe Stop 1 and the other drive safety functions realize the industrial stop categories is developed in @sec-enforcement-stop-categories.
:::

Any hardware split must keep the permission path the sole writer of the actuators and bound its check time across all expected hardware and software faults. Putting the two paths on separate chips is the cleanest way to start, though empirical timing evidence under load must still confirm that isolation. Separate processors, however, run on asynchronous clocks at very different rates, so the link between them must pass trajectory updates continuously without ever forcing the fast permission reader to wait on the slower host writer.

## Multi-Rate Cadences {#sec-nervous-cadences}

A motor drive cannot wait for the next camera-based proposal before regulating winding current. Conversely, forcing a learned policy to evaluate at current-loop rates wastes compute without generating fresher sensory observations. Decoupling these cadences allows each workload to meet its distinct physical or computational deadline, provided the boundary interface preserves data freshness and never blocks local real-time control.

### Physical time constants and sampling phase lag {#sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag}

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-machine-tiers
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE RUNNING MACHINE'S RATE TIERS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-cadences, the four-tier sentence, the perception
# │          paragraph, and the chunk-policy tier paragraph.
# │ Goal:    Give the machine's own proposer rates and chunk horizon, and the
# │          base's travel during one camera exposure.
# │ Show:    chunk policy 20 Hz (50 ms = 2 x 25 ms setpoints, M5), intent model
# │          2 Hz (500 ms), H = 16; permission tick 1 kHz (1000 us, +/- 10 us
# │          release jitter, illustrative); 22.5 mm of base
# │          travel in a 15 ms exposure at the 1.5 m/s drive limit.
# │ How:     Rates and horizon from RM; travel = drive limit x exposure, with
# │          the exposure a scenario input.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_frequency, fmt_int, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class MachineTiers:
    """Proposer rates, chunk horizon, and exposure travel on the running machine."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen (chunk-policy renewal rate)
    f_intent = RM.intent_rate  # category: chosen (intent-model rate)
    chunk_horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen (setpoints per chunk)
    chunk_step = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen (setpoint step)
    f_current = RM.current_loop_rate  # category: chosen (drive current-loop rate)
    f_perm = RM.permission_rate  # category: chosen (permission tick)
    t_tick_jitter = 10 * microsecond  # category: illustrative (release-jitter allowance of the tick; scenario assumption)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    t_exp = 15 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (exposure in a 300 lux scene; scenario assumption)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_exp = (v * t_exp).to(millimeter)
    t_chunk_period = RM.chunk_period  # renewal period, a whole number of setpoint steps
    n_per_renewal = RM.chunk_schedule["setpoints_per_renewal"]
    t_current = (1 / f_current).to(microsecond)  # current-loop sampling period
    t_perm = (1 / f_perm).to(microsecond)  # permission-tick period

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_current.to(kHz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Current-loop rate drifted: {f_current}")
    # margin_cadence_tier_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 500 ms, 50 ms, 1 ms, 50 us.
    check(abs(t_current.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"Current-loop period drifted: {t_current}")
    check(abs(RM.chunk_period.to(millisecond).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Ladder: chunk period drifted")
    check(abs((1 / f_intent).to(millisecond).magnitude - 500.0) < 1e-9, "Ladder: intent period drifted")
    # The ladder caption says each tier runs at least ten times faster than the one above it.
    check(
        f_current >= 10 * RM.permission_rate and RM.permission_rate * RM.chunk_period >= 10 and RM.chunk_period * 10 <= 1 / f_intent,
        "Ladder caption: tier ratio fell below ten",
    )
    check(abs(f_chunk.to(hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk rate drifted: {f_chunk}")
    check(abs(f_intent.to(hertz).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Intent rate drifted: {f_intent}")
    check(abs(t_perm.magnitude - 1000.0) < 1e-9, f"Permission-tick period drifted: {t_perm}")
    check(t_tick_jitter <= 0.01 * t_perm, "Tick release jitter must be small against the period.")
    check(chunk_horizon == 16, f"Chunk horizon drifted: {chunk_horizon}")
    check(abs(chunk_step.to(millisecond).magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-9, f"Setpoint step drifted: {chunk_step}")
    check(n_per_renewal == 2, f"Setpoints per renewal drifted: {n_per_renewal}")
    check(abs(v.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Drive limit drifted: {v}")
    check(abs(d_exp.magnitude - 22.5) < 1e-9, f"Exposure travel drifted: {d_exp}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    f_chunk_str = fmt_frequency(f_chunk, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    f_intent_str = fmt_frequency(f_intent, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_intent_period_str = fmt_latency((1 / f_intent).to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_horizon_str = fmt_int(chunk_horizon)
    chunk_step_str = fmt_latency(chunk_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_current_str = fmt_frequency(f_current, unit=kHz, precision=0)
    t_current_str = fmt_latency(t_current, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    f_perm_str = fmt_frequency(f_perm.to(kHz), unit=kHz, precision=0)
    t_perm_str = fmt_latency(t_perm, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_tick_jitter_str = fmt_latency(t_tick_jitter, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    n_per_renewal_str = fmt_int(n_per_renewal)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    t_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_exp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_exp_str = fmt_length(d_exp, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

The mobile manipulator's motor inverters regulate winding current every `{python} MachineTiers.t_current_str` (`{python} MachineTiers.f_current_str`), while its chunk policy requires `{python} MachineStallTravel.t_chunk_str` at p99 latency to ingest camera frames and generate an action chunk. No single cadence can serve both the winding's electromagnetic dynamics and the cost of deep visual inference. The four tiers named in @sec-nervous-multi-rate-bridge therefore each take their rate from a different time constant:

1. **Inner Commutation and Current Loop (`{python} MachineTiers.f_current_str`, `{python} MachineTiers.t_current_str` cycle):** The PWM carrier frequency, selected to balance switching losses, current ripple, and acoustic noise, fixes the sampling instants. Phase currents are sampled once per carrier period at its midpoint, so a `{python} MachineTiers.f_current_str` carrier yields $\SamplingPeriod =$ `{python} MachineTiers.t_current_str`. The stator winding's electrical time constant establishes the plant pole that the current regulator must compensate. For the hub motors, $\ElectricalTimeConstant = \PhaseInductance/\PhaseResistance =$ `{python} WindingTimeConstant.tau_e_str` (@sec-body-electrical-time-constants) places that pole near `{python} WindingTimeConstant.f_pole_str`. The closed-loop current bandwidth is tuned well above this pole and at least a factor of ten below the sampling rate, reaching at most about `{python} WindingTimeConstant.f_bw_cap_str` [@franklin1998digital]. This loop executes directly within drive silicon and commands electromagnetic torque through the motor controller.
2. **Permission and Position-Supervision Tick (`{python} MachineTiers.f_perm_str`, `{python} MachineTiers.t_perm_str` $\pm$ `{python} MachineTiers.t_tick_jitter_str` cycle):** The rate here is set by distance rather than by a plant pole. Each tick of detection delay is base travel the stopping budget must absorb, and each tick must also supply the drives a fresh position setpoint. At one tick per millisecond both demands are met with the margins quantified below, while the drives close the subordinate velocity and current loops.
3. **Action-Chunk Policy Stream (`{python} MachineTiers.f_chunk_str`, `{python} MachineTiers.t_chunk_period_str` cycle):** Bridging observation age and mechanical execution, the local policy emits receding-horizon action chunks ($\ActionChunkHorizon =$ `{python} MachineTiers.chunk_horizon_str` waypoints spaced `{python} MachineTiers.chunk_step_str` apart). On this machine, the policy is a compact visuomotor network following the Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) architecture, which decodes an entire chunk in a single forward pass; @sec-brain-action-chunking priced it against the iterative diffusion and flow-matching heads that trade more passes for expressiveness. Each pass must stream the model's weights from memory on the application processor's accelerator, which caps the pass rate near $\PolicyPassRate \le \SustainedMemoryBandwidth/\WeightMemory$. Because one pass yields all `{python} MachineTiers.chunk_horizon_str` setpoints, that sweep is paid once per chunk rather than once per setpoint, which is what lets the policy renew at this rate.
4. **Multimodal Intent Planner (`{python} MachineTiers.f_intent_str`, `{python} MachineTiers.t_intent_period_str` cycle):** A high-capacity VLA model turns camera frames and a natural-language instruction into task goals and navigation targets. Its period is set by the prefill and weight sweeps of @sec-brain-memory-wall, not by any plant dynamics, which is why it may steer the chunk policy but never hold a chunk lease, the authority to keep driving the actuators that @sec-nervous-lease-sizing sizes in tens of milliseconds.

The two proposer cadences reflect mainstream action-chunking and VLA architectures as of 2026, and their frequencies will shift as models and accelerators evolve. The method developed below does not depend on them. It anchors the lease's lower limit to what the proposer can supply and its upper limit to the physical stopping budget.

The current-loop rate follows directly from the winding's electrical time constant $\PhaseInductance/\PhaseResistance$, and the loop closes within the drive's local inverter. The harder timing question arises one level up, at the joint. There, inertia and structural compliance set the required closed-loop bandwidth, and every digital stage between sensor and actuator (sampling, computation, bus transport) exacts a penalty in phase lag. The crossover frequency $\CrossoverFrequency$ marks the point where open-loop gain equals unity. At this frequency, the phase margin[^fn-phase-margin-bode] defines the maximum additional phase lag the system can absorb before feedback transitions from stabilizing attenuation to self-reinforcing oscillation.

[^fn-phase-margin-bode]: **Phase Margin**: @bode1945network introduced gain and phase margins to measure how far a feedback amplifier sits from instability, turning the stability criterion of @nyquist1932regeneration into a practical design margin. In cyber-physical loops, delay erodes the modeled phase reserve and can destabilize the loop under its nominal assumptions. Establishing actual damping and stability requires the complete sampled plant, compensation, and timing response. Because a pure transport or compute delay $\PureTransportDelay$ subtracts $\CrossoverFrequency \PureTransportDelay$ radians of phase regardless of cause, bus cycles, compute stages, and zero-order holds all draw from the same finite phase budget. \index{Phase margin!delay budget}

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-tick-delay-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TOTAL-DELAY PHASE BUDGET FOR A LOOP CLOSED THROUGH THE TICK (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag, the delay-budget paragraphs.
# │ Goal:    Show that a 20 Hz joint loop closed across the permission tick
# │          and fieldbus exceeds the chosen phase erosion allowance (M1).
# │ Show:    ZOH 3.6 deg + bus 7.2 deg + compute 1.8 deg = 12.6 deg against a
# │          5 deg allowance (0.69 ms of total delay); next-tick output 18.0 deg;
# │          highest crossover at 1 kHz 7.9 Hz; 500 Hz ZOH alone 7.2 deg;
# │          1.5 mm of base travel per millisecond of detection delay.
# │ How:     calc_phase_lag_total (appendix_control total-delay formula);
# │          tick, bus, WCET from AISLE; crossover and allowance chosen.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_multiple, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class TickDelayBudget:
    """Phase erosion of a joint loop closed through the permission tick and the bus."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    f_c = 20.0 * hertz  # category: chosen (illustrative joint-loop crossover)
    phi_allow = 5.0 * degree  # category: chosen (illustrative erosion allowance)
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen (1 kHz permission tick)
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative (EtherCAT cycle)
    t_comp = AISLE.enforcer_wcet  # category: chosen (declared enforcer WCET)
    t_tick_slow = 2.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (500 Hz comparison)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    same_tick = calc_phase_lag_total(f_c, t_tick, compute_delay=t_comp, transport_delay=t_bus, phase_allowance=phi_allow)
    next_tick = calc_phase_lag_total(f_c, t_tick, compute_delay=t_tick, transport_delay=t_bus, phase_allowance=phi_allow)
    slow_zoh = calc_phase_lag_total(f_c, t_tick_slow)
    phi_zoh = same_tick["phase_zoh"].to(degree).magnitude
    phi_bus = same_tick["phase_transport"].to(degree).magnitude
    phi_comp = same_tick["phase_compute"].to(degree).magnitude
    phi_total = same_tick["phase_total"].to(degree).magnitude
    phi_next = next_tick["phase_total"].to(degree).magnitude
    phi_slow = slow_zoh["phase_zoh"].to(degree).magnitude
    tau_total = same_tick["tau_total"].to(millisecond)
    tau_next = next_tick["tau_total"].to(millisecond)
    tau_allowed = same_tick["tau_allowed"].to(millisecond)
    f_max = same_tick["f_crossover_max"].to(hertz)
    over_ratio = phi_total / phi_allow.magnitude
    mm_per_ms = (v * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)
    n_fir = 9  # category: illustrative (moving-average taps, fn-fir-smoothing)
    tau_fir = ((n_fir - 1) / 2 * t_tick).to(millisecond)  # FIR group delay, (N-1)/2 samples
    phi_fir = (360.0 * f_c * tau_fir).to(dimensionless).magnitude  # degrees at crossover

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_fir.magnitude - 4.0) < 1e-9, f"FIR group delay drifted: {tau_fir}")
    check(abs(phi_fir - 28.8) < 1e-9, f"FIR phase at crossover drifted: {phi_fir}")
    # margin_tick_phase_budget_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 20 Hz, 5, 3.6, 1.8, 7.2, 12.6 degrees (guarded here).
    check(abs(phi_zoh - 3.6) < 1e-9, f"ZOH phase drifted: {phi_zoh}")
    check(abs(phi_bus - 7.2) < 1e-9, f"Bus phase drifted: {phi_bus}")
    check(abs(phi_comp - 1.8) < 1e-9, f"Compute phase drifted: {phi_comp}")
    check(abs(phi_total - 12.6) < 1e-9, f"Total phase drifted: {phi_total}")
    check(abs(phi_next - 18.0) < 1e-9, f"Next-tick total phase drifted: {phi_next}")
    check(abs(phi_slow - 7.2) < 1e-9, f"500 Hz ZOH phase drifted: {phi_slow}")
    check(phi_zoh < phi_allow.magnitude < phi_bus, "ZOH alone fits the allowance; the bus alone does not")
    check(t_bus > tau_allowed, "The bus cycle alone exceeds the whole delay allowance")
    check(abs(f_max.magnitude - 7.9365) < 1e-3, f"Highest supported crossover drifted: {f_max}")
    check(abs(mm_per_ms.magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Travel per millisecond drifted: {mm_per_ms}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    f_c_str = fmt_frequency(f_c, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    phi_allow_str = fmt(phi_allow.magnitude, precision=0)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_comp_str = fmt_latency(t_comp.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    phi_zoh_str = fmt(phi_zoh, precision=1)
    phi_bus_str = fmt(phi_bus, precision=1)
    phi_comp_str = fmt(phi_comp, precision=1)
    phi_total_str = fmt(phi_total, precision=1)
    phi_next_str = fmt(phi_next, precision=0)
    phi_slow_str = fmt(phi_slow, precision=1)
    tau_total_str = fmt_latency(tau_total, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    tau_next_str = fmt_latency(tau_next, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    tau_allowed_str = fmt_latency(tau_allowed, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    f_max_str = fmt_frequency(f_max, unit=hertz, precision=1)
    over_mult_str = fmt_multiple(over_ratio, precision=1)
    mm_per_ms_str = fmt_length(mm_per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    n_fir_str = fmt(n_fir, precision=0)
    tau_fir_str = fmt_latency(tau_fir, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    phi_fir_str = fmt(phi_fir, precision=1)
    fir_over_mult_str = fmt_multiple(phi_fir / phi_allow.magnitude, precision=1)
```

Excess phase lag causes corrective control torques to arrive out of phase with physical joint motion, eventually turning stabilizing negative feedback into unstable positive feedback [@nyquist1932regeneration]. Closing a feedback loop across the permission tick accumulates three distinct sources of latency. The discrete sample-and-hold introduces an effective transport delay equal to half the sample period ($\SamplingPeriod/2$); the enforcer requires compute time ($\EnforcerComputeTime$) to evaluate constraints; and the resulting command incurs fieldbus transit latency ($\CommandTransportTime$) before reaching the drive. Because a pure delay $\PureTransportDelay$ removes $\AngularFrequency \PureTransportDelay$ radians of phase across all frequencies, these stages collectively erode the phase margin at crossover according to @eq-nervous-delay-phase, the total-delay relation given in @sec-appendix-control-zoh:
$$\DelayPhaseLag = \CrossoverFrequency\left(\frac{\SamplingPeriod}{2} + \EnforcerComputeTime + \CommandTransportTime\right)$$ {#eq-nervous-delay-phase}

Consider an illustrative joint-loop crossover of `{python} TickDelayBudget.f_c_str` and a design phase erosion allowance of `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_allow_str`$^\circ$. A `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_tick_str` tick's sample-and-hold accounts for `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_zoh_str`$^\circ$, which fits comfortably within the budget. However, the `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_bus_str` fieldbus transit cycle contributes `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_bus_str`$^\circ$ on its own, and the enforcer's declared worst-case execution time of `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_comp_str` adds another `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_comp_str`$^\circ$. The combined delay of `{python} TickDelayBudget.tau_total_str` imposes `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_total_str`$^\circ$ of phase lag, `{python} TickDelayBudget.over_mult_str` the allowance. If the controller delays output release until the subsequent tick boundary, total phase erosion escalates to `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_next_str`$^\circ$ over `{python} TickDelayBudget.tau_next_str`. Because the phase budget tolerates at most `{python} TickDelayBudget.tau_allowed_str` of total delay, less than a single bus cycle, no increase in tick frequency can keep a `{python} TickDelayBudget.f_c_str` loop closed across this communication bus within its erosion allowance. The loop might remain stable, but it would spend phase margin the design never allocated to delay. Given `{python} TickDelayBudget.tau_total_str` of unavoidable transit and processing latency, a `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_tick_str` tick stays within the chosen phase erosion allowance only at crossover frequencies no greater than `{python} TickDelayBudget.f_max_str`. Reducing the tick rate to $500\text{ Hz}$ increases the sample-and-hold penalty alone to `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_slow_str`$^\circ$, whereas driving the tick frequency toward infinity still leaves the bus transport penalty untouched. Loop placement, rather than clock scaling, resolves this architectural constraint.

::: {.column-margin}
<!-- fig-alt hand-types the phase terms; TickDelayBudget guards them (3.6, 1.8, 7.2, 12.6 against 5 degrees).
     Drawn by generate_margin_figures.py (ch04_phase_budget_envelope); --check fails on drift. -->
![](images/svg/margin_tick_phase_budget_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One stacked horizontal bar of phase lag at a 20 hertz crossover: hold 3.6 degrees, compute 1.8 degrees, and bus 7.2 degrees, totaling 12.6 degrees. A dashed red line at 5 degrees allowed falls inside the compute segment, and the whole bus segment lies in the shaded region past it."}

*The bus cycle alone spends more phase than the loop can spare.*
:::

Consequently, the machine closes its high-rate joint velocity and current loops directly within the decentralized motor drives, where co-located encoder sampling bypasses the fieldbus entirely. The centralized `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_tick_str` permission tick operates strictly as a supervisor and trajectory setpoint generator. This decouples the tick from joint-level phase margin constraints, replacing them with two distinct systems requirements. First, as a safety supervisor, each millisecond of detection delay incurs `{python} TickDelayBudget.mm_per_ms_str` of unbraked base travel at maximum drive velocity, directly consuming clearance from the stopping budget (notebook \ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}). Second, as a setpoint source, the tick must evaluate the admitted trajectory frequently enough to supply smooth kinematic references to the drives. Transport delay along this reference path introduces tracking lag rather than eroding the drive loop's phase margin, because the reference sits outside the feedback loop. Any outer supervisory corrections closed across the bus, such as cartesian compliance trims, must restrict their crossover bandwidth below `{python} TickDelayBudget.f_max_str`.

Closing those loops in the drive is a hardware arrangement rather than merely a firmware setting. The fastest loop sits beside its sensor and its switch, so phase current is measured and switched next to the winding with no host processor in the loop, and dedicated PWM timers in the same silicon enforce the gap between complementary switch transitions that keeps the power bridge from shorting.[^fn-hw-epwm-deadtime] The running machine's brushless hub drives follow this arrangement at a larger scale; the small stepper-motor driver of @fig-real-motor-controller shows it on one chip.

[^fn-hw-epwm-deadtime]: **Dead-Time Delay**\index{Dead-time delay}: The interval in which both switches of a half-bridge leg are off, so the leg never shorts the DC bus, is the inverter dead time introduced in @sec-body-electrical-time-constants. Dedicated pulse-width modulation timers insert it in hardware ($100\text{--}500\text{ ns}$) on every transition, and drive firmware applies online volt-second compensation for the voltage error it introduces.

::: {#fig-real-motor-controller fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Integrated motor-driver silicon**: A Trinamic TMC2209 stepper-motor driver in a quad flat no-lead (QFN) package, with a low-value current-sense resistor (marked R110) beside it on the board. The chip carries its own power transistors and current regulation, so the winding current is measured and switched next to the motor it drives rather than by the host processor. A photograph shows the placement; the timing of the current loop is a property of the silicon that the datasheet and measurement must establish. (Photo: Phiarc, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Trinamic_TMC2209_stepper_motor_controller_chip.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0)." fig-alt="Macro photograph of a square QFN integrated circuit marked TMC2209-LA on a black printed circuit board, with a larger surface-mount resistor marked R110 at upper left and small capacitors and copper traces around it."}
![](images/jpg/fig04_real_motor_drive_controller.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

Perception pipelines feeding the policy stream execute at intermediate cadences constrained by optical physics, sensor exposure durations, and relative scene velocity. In a typical $300\text{ lux}$ warehouse lighting environment requiring a `{python} MachineTiers.t_exp_str` exposure, the robot base traveling at its `{python} MachineTiers.v_str` drive limit covers $\ExposureTravelDistance = \SpeedAtDetection\,\ExposureDuration =$ `{python} MachineTiers.d_exp_str` while the shutter is open. Resulting image-plane blur interacts with scene depth and optical geometry, setting physical limits on feature tracking. The achievable signal-to-noise ratio, spatial motion blur, and image preprocessing latency jointly establish the feasible sensing cadence for visual control, a trade-off @sec-perception develops. For the permission path the exposure matters as time. An observation is dated at its exposure midpoint, so half the exposure is already part of its age before any processing begins, and that age is the first interval the lease budget must charge (@tbl-04-event-timing).

The chunk-policy generation rate must satisfy the proposal-supply budget set in @sec-brain-action-chunking. For our mobile manipulator, a `{python} MachineTiers.f_chunk_str` renewal cycle paired with an $\ActionChunkHorizon =$ `{python} MachineTiers.chunk_horizon_str` waypoint horizon [@zhao2023learning] bridges visual perception and high-rate actuation. The `{python} MachineTiers.t_chunk_period_str` renewal period matches `{python} MachineTiers.n_per_renewal_str` discrete setpoint steps of `{python} MachineTiers.chunk_step_str`, so every scheduled renewal lands on a setpoint boundary, provided the handoff between the two clocks never makes the faster reader wait.

### Lock-free and wait-free mailbox exchanges {#sec-nervous-mailbox-exchanges}

If a `{python} MachineTiers.f_perm_str` safety loop blocks on a mutual exclusion lock held by a `{python} MachineTiers.f_chunk_str` neural network runtime, one page fault or scheduling hiccup in the runtime becomes an unbounded priority inversion, and the hard real-time controller misses its cycle deadline. Because the tiers run on different processors at different rates, every exchange across a rate boundary must give the faster reader bounded, nonblocking access. Panel (b) of @fig-04-multirate-cadence-buffer follows the remedy developed here, the mailbox, through a clean exchange, a write preempted by the tick, and a stalled host, and in none of the three does the reader wait. Panel (a), which shows what the tick does when the proposer stops renewing altogether, returns in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing once the lease that governs it is defined.

Standard inter-process communication libraries rarely provide deterministic execution bounds out of the box. Message serialization, dynamic memory allocation, intermediate queueing, and thread scheduling can each introduce unpredictable delivery stalls. While shared memory eliminates buffer copying and kernel context switches, it requires concurrency controls to prevent the reader from ingesting partially written, inconsistent command payloads. The communication protocol must strictly bound the consumer's execution time, even when the producer stalls at the most unfavorable point in its write cycle.

While a first-in, first-out (FIFO) queue guarantees sequential message delivery, message ordering is the wrong semantic model for physical motion control. If the control consumer falls behind the rate of production, queued motion plans represent progressively stale physical state estimates. Backpressure, the queue's way of slowing a producer, cannot pause moving mass. The real-time enforcer requires the freshest complete proposal, paired with a strict temporal deadline. This principle does not prevent the controller from buffering the future waypoints of an already admitted trajectory; those waypoints follow an explicit execution schedule governed by a valid lease. Rather, it prevents treating the delayed consumption of historical commands as valid control inputs. Real-time distributed systems distinguish these two communication semantics. An *event message*\index{Event message} is queued and consumed exactly once, where dropping a message loses state history, whereas a *state message*\index{State message} represents current environmental state and updates in place, allowing new observations to overwrite older ones without queuing [@kopetz2011real]. The proposal mailbox implements state-message semantics via a single-slot seqlock, following the non-blocking write protocol of @kopetz1993nbw to ensure mutual independence between writer progress and reader execution.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-multirate-stall
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LEGO VALUES FOR @fig-04-multirate-cadence-buffer
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: caption of @fig-04-multirate-cadence-buffer and its plotting cell.
# │ Goal:    Compute and guard the values the caption prints, before the
# │          figure div, so the caption can reference them.
# │ How:     See the class docstring; every value from RM / AISLE.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class MultirateStall:
    """One proposer stall on the running machine's clocks, drawn to scale."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_renew = RM.chunk_period.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (M5)
    t_infer = RM.chunk_inference_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (P99)
    t_step = RM.chunk_step.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (M5)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus.to(millisecond)  # category: derived (fieldbus cycle)
    t_onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Renewals begin at 0, T, 2T; the third never completes (the stall).
    t_last_adm = t_renew + t_infer  # last admission
    t_expiry = t_last_adm + t_lease  # lease lapses
    t_brake = t_expiry + t_tick + t_bus + t_onset
    renewal_to_onset = (t_brake - t_last_adm).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_last_adm.magnitude - 90.0) < 1e-9, f"Last admission drifted: {t_last_adm}")
    check(abs(t_expiry.magnitude - 150.0) < 1e-9, f"Lease expiry drifted: {t_expiry}")
    check(abs(renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, f"Renewal-to-onset drifted: {renewal_to_onset}")
    check(t_renew + (t_renew - t_infer) / 2 < t_lease, "The lease must outlast one renewal period")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_renew_str = fmt_latency(t_renew, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_infer_str = fmt_latency(t_infer, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_step_str = fmt_latency(t_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
```

::: {#fig-04-multirate-cadence-buffer fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Multi-rate cadence and the mailbox exchange**: (a) The running machine's clocks during a proposer stall, to scale. The chunk policy renews every `{python} MultirateStall.t_renew_str` and needs `{python} MultirateStall.t_infer_str`; the admitted chunk supplies a setpoint every `{python} MultirateStall.t_step_str`. When the third renewal never completes, the tick keeps executing the admitted chunk only until the `{python} MultirateStall.t_lease_str` lease from the last admission lapses; the tick, bus, and brake onset then put the fallback stop `{python} MultirateStall.renewal_to_onset_str` after that admission. (b) The single-slot seqlock in the microcontroller's own memory, in event order. The receive interrupt makes the counter odd, copies a checked frame, and makes it even; the tick accepts a copy only when it reads the same even value before and after. A tick that preempts a write reads an odd value and keeps its last validated chunk, and a stalled application processor leaves the slot unchanged while the lease runs." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel a, a timeline from 0 to about 210 milliseconds with five lanes. Chunk policy: inference bars from 0 to 40 and 50 to 90, then a hatched stalled bar from 100 onward. Setpoints: ticks every 25 milliseconds from 40 to 140. Lease: a dashed outline from 40 to 100 and a filled bar from 90 to 150 labeled lease 60 ms from last admission. Permission tick: fine lines every 1 millisecond. Drives: tracking until 150, a short green interval to 172 labeled tick plus bus plus onset 22 ms, then a red fallback stop. Dashed vertical lines mark last admission at 90, lease expiry at 150, and a red brake onset at 172. Panel b, three lanes in event order: receive ISR writer, sequence counter, and permission tick reader, in three cases. Clean exchange: the writer copies a frame while the counter goes 7 then 8, and the reader reads 8 twice and accepts. Tick preempts a write: the counter reads 9 during a paused write, the reader rejects, then after the counter becomes 10 the reader accepts. Application processor stalls: no frame arrives and the reader reads 10 again twice."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-04-multirate-cadence-buffer
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MULTI-RATE CADENCE AND THE MCU-LOCAL SEQLOCK (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-04-multirate-cadence-buffer in @sec-nervous-mailbox-exchanges.
