```{python}
# │ Goal:    (a) Show a proposer stall on the machine's own clocks, to scale:
# │          renewal, setpoint supply, lease, tick, and the fallback stop.
# │          (b) Show the single-slot seqlock on the MCU: the receive interrupt
# │          writes, the tick reads, and parity rejects a torn read.
# │ Show:    renewals every 50 ms with 40 ms inference; setpoints every 25 ms;
# │          last admission 90 ms; lease 60 ms to expiry at 150 ms; tick + bus
# │          + onset to brake onset 82 ms after the last admission.
# │ How:     RM.chunk_period / chunk_inference_latency / chunk_step and
# │          AISLE.t_lease / t_tick / t_bus / t_brake_onset (M5). Panel (b) is
# │          an event-order schematic with no time scale.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

M = MultirateStall
R = viz.VOL4_ROLES
tint = lambda c, a: tuple(1 - a * (1 - int(c[i : i + 2], 16) / 255) for i in (1, 3, 5))
renew, infer, step = M.t_renew.magnitude, M.t_infer.magnitude, M.t_step.magnitude
adm, exp_, brake = M.t_last_adm.magnitude, M.t_expiry.magnitude, M.t_brake.magnitude
tick = M.t_tick.magnitude
x1 = brake + 38

viz.set_book_style()
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.4, 8.6), gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1.4, 1], hspace=0.36))

# ── (a) cadences, to scale ────────────────────────────────────────────────
lanes = ["chunk policy", "setpoints", "lease", "permission tick", "drives"]
y = {name: len(lanes) - 1 - i for i, name in enumerate(lanes)}
H = 0.52
for i, name in enumerate(lanes):
    if i % 2 == 0:
        ax.axhspan(y[name] - 0.5, y[name] + 0.5, color="#F4F6F9", lw=0, zorder=0)
for k in range(2):
    t0 = k * renew
    ax.barh(y["chunk policy"], infer, left=t0, height=H, color=tint(R["proposal"], 0.22), ec=R["proposal"], lw=1, zorder=3)
    ax.text(t0 + infer / 2, y["chunk policy"], f"infer {infer:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color=R["proposal"], zorder=4)
    ax.plot([t0 + infer] * 2, [-0.5, len(lanes) - 0.5], color=R["proposal"], lw=0.8, ls=(0, (1, 2)), zorder=2)
ax.barh(y["chunk policy"], x1 - 2 * renew, left=2 * renew, height=H, color="white", ec=R["proposal"], lw=1, hatch="///", zorder=3)
ax.text(
    2 * renew + 3,
    y["chunk policy"],
    "stalled",
    ha="left",
    va="center",
    fontsize=9,
    color=R["proposal"],
    zorder=4,
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="square,pad=0.1", fc="white", ec="none"),
)
t = infer
while t <= exp_ + 1e-9:
    ax.plot([t, t], [y["setpoints"] - H / 2, y["setpoints"] + H / 2], color=R["structural"], lw=2.2, zorder=3)
    t += step
ax.text(1, y["setpoints"], f"every {step:.0f} ms", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=9, color=R["structural"])
ax.barh(y["lease"], M.t_lease.magnitude, left=infer, height=H * 0.55, color="white", ec=R["structural"], lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=3)
ax.barh(y["lease"], M.t_lease.magnitude, left=adm, height=H, color=tint(R["structural"], 0.25), ec=R["structural"], lw=1, zorder=4)
ax.text(
    adm + M.t_lease.magnitude / 2,
    y["lease"],
    f"lease {M.t_lease.magnitude:.0f} ms from\nlast admission",
    linespacing=1.0,
    ha="center",
    va="center",
    fontsize=9,
    color=R["structural"],
    zorder=5,
)
ax.axhspan(y["permission tick"] - H / 2, y["permission tick"] + H / 2, xmin=0, xmax=1, color=tint(R["structural"], 0.12), lw=0, zorder=1)
tt = 0.0
while tt <= x1:
    ax.plot([tt, tt], [y["permission tick"] - H / 2, y["permission tick"] + H / 2], color=R["structural"], lw=0.35, alpha=0.7, zorder=2)
    tt += tick
ax.text(x1 - 2, y["permission tick"] + H / 2 + 0.06, f"every {tick:.0f} ms", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=R["structural"])
ax.barh(y["drives"], exp_, left=0, height=H, color=tint(R["neutral"], 0.15), ec=R["neutral"], lw=0.9, zorder=3)
ax.text(infer / 2, y["drives"], "tracking", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color=R["neutral"], zorder=4)
ax.barh(y["drives"], brake - exp_, left=exp_, height=H, color=tint(R["structural"], 0.35), ec=R["structural"], lw=0.9, zorder=3)
ax.barh(y["drives"], x1 - brake, left=brake, height=H, color=R["consequence"], ec=R["consequence"], lw=0.9, zorder=3)
ax.text(brake + (x1 - brake) / 2, y["drives"], "fallback stop", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color="white", zorder=4)
ax.annotate(
    f"tick + bus + onset {brake - exp_:.0f} ms",
    xy=((exp_ + brake) / 2, y["drives"] - H / 2),
    xytext=((exp_ + brake) / 2 - 30, y["drives"] - 0.78),
    fontsize=9,
    color=R["structural"],
    ha="center",
    va="top",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=R["structural"], lw=0.7),
)
for tx, lab, c, ha in [
    (adm, "last admission", R["structural"], "center"),
    (exp_, "lease expiry", R["structural"], "center"),
    (brake, "brake onset", R["consequence"], "left"),
]:
    ax.plot([tx, tx], [-0.5, len(lanes) - 0.5 + 0.12], color=c, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=2)
    ax.text(tx, len(lanes) - 0.5 + 0.16, lab, ha=ha, va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=c, bbox=dict(boxstyle="square,pad=0.06", fc="white", ec="none"))
ax.set_xlim(-4, x1)
ax.set_ylim(-1.3, len(lanes) - 0.5 + 0.7)
ax.set_yticks([y[n] for n in lanes])
ax.set_yticklabels(lanes, fontsize=9)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
ax.grid(False)
for s in ("left", "right", "top"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel("Time from the first renewal (ms)")
ax.text(-0.13, 1.06, "(a)", transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", va="bottom")

# ── (b) seqlock on the MCU, schematic ────────────────────────────────────
blanes = ["receive ISR\n(writer)", "sequence\ncounter", "permission tick\n(reader)"]
by = {name: 2 - i for i, name in enumerate(blanes)}
for i, name in enumerate(blanes):
    if i % 2 == 0:
        bx.axhspan(by[name] - 0.5, by[name] + 0.5, color="#F4F6F9", lw=0, zorder=0)
bh = 0.5

def wbar(a, b, lab=""):
    bx.barh(by["receive ISR\n(writer)"], b - a, left=a, height=bh, color=tint(R["proposal"], 0.22), ec=R["proposal"], lw=1, zorder=3)
    if lab:
        bx.text((a + b) / 2, by["receive ISR\n(writer)"] + bh / 2 + 0.05, lab, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=R["proposal"], zorder=4)

def rbar(a, b, lab, ok):
    c = R["structural"]
    bx.barh(
        by["permission tick\n(reader)"],
        b - a,
        left=a,
        height=bh,
        color=tint(c, 0.25) if ok else "white",
        ec=c,
        lw=1,
        hatch=None if ok else "///",
        zorder=3,
    )
    bx.text((a + b) / 2, by["permission tick\n(reader)"] - bh / 2 - 0.06, lab, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=9, color=c, zorder=4)

def cval(t, v):
    odd = v % 2 == 1
    bx.text(
        t,
        by["sequence\ncounter"],
        str(v),
        ha="center",
        va="center",
        fontsize=9,
        fontweight="bold",
        color="white" if odd else R["neutral"],
        zorder=4,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="square,pad=0.3", fc=R["neutral"] if odd else "white", ec=R["neutral"], lw=0.8),
    )

# case 1: clean write, then clean read
wbar(0.6, 2.0, "copy frame")
cval(0.6, 7)
cval(2.0, 8)
rbar(3.0, 4.2, "read 8 ... 8:\naccept", True)
# case 2: tick preempts a write in progress
wbar(5.6, 6.2)
wbar(7.4, 8.2)
cval(5.6, 9)
cval(8.2, 10)
bx.plot([6.2, 7.4], [by["receive ISR\n(writer)"]] * 2, color=R["proposal"], lw=1, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=2)
bx.text(6.8, by["receive ISR\n(writer)"] + bh / 2 + 0.05, "preempted", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=R["proposal"])
rbar(6.2, 7.4, "read 9, odd:\nreject", False)
rbar(9.0, 10.2, "read 10 ... 10:\naccept", True)
# case 3: no frames arrive
rbar(12.0, 13.2, "read 10\nagain", True)
rbar(14.4, 15.6, "read 10\nagain", True)
bx.text(
    13.8,
    by["receive ISR\n(writer)"],
    "no frame arrives;\nthe lease keeps running",
    ha="center",
    va="center",
    fontsize=9,
    color=R["neutral"],
    style="italic",
)
for xa, lab in [(0.2, "clean exchange"), (5.2, "tick preempts a write"), (11.6, "application processor stalls")]:
    bx.text(xa, 2.72, lab, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=R["neutral"])
for xs in (4.8, 11.0):
    bx.plot([xs, xs], [-0.95, 2.95], color="#CBD5E1", lw=0.8, zorder=1)
bx.set_xlim(0, 16.2)
bx.set_ylim(-1.0, 3.05)
bx.set_yticks([by[n] for n in blanes])
bx.set_yticklabels(blanes, fontsize=9)
bx.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
bx.set_xticks([])
bx.grid(False)
for s in ("left", "right", "top"):
    bx.spines[s].set_visible(False)
bx.set_xlabel("Event order on the MCU (not to scale)")
bx.text(-0.13, 1.02, "(b)", transform=bx.transAxes, fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", va="bottom")
plt.show()
```
:::

A baseline nonblocking exchange uses a **single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) seqlock mailbox**\index{Sequence lock}[^fn-seqlock-versioned-read] in the microcontroller's own static memory. The proposal first crosses the board-level link as a framed packet, which a DMA transfer lands in a private receive buffer. A receive interrupt outside the tick checks the frame's CRC and sequence number and copies the proposal into the mailbox slot. Both participants therefore execute on the microcontroller, the receive interrupt as writer and the permission tick as reader, and the application processor never touches mailbox memory.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The boundary contract that keeps the application processor out of the microcontroller's mailbox memory is developed in @sec-placement-boundary-contract.
:::

[^fn-seqlock-versioned-read]: **Versioned Read**: @lamport1977concurrent showed that a reader can detect a concurrent, overlapping write without acquiring mutual exclusion locks. By incrementing a version counter before and after updating payload data, and having the reader sample the counter in reverse order, any mismatch reliably flags a torn read. \index{Sequence lock!Lamport versioned read}

The writer increments the sequence counter to an odd value, copies the checked frame into the slot, and increments the counter to an even value using store-release memory ordering. The reader makes exactly one bounded read attempt per control cycle and rejects the snapshot if the counter begins odd or changes before the read finishes. A snapshot that passes becomes the active chunk only after its integrity, freshness, and physical-admissibility checks succeed, and the tick then interpolates it into setpoints (@sec-nervous-rate-interpolation). A rejected read leaves the previously admitted chunk in force, so the reader never blocks on the writer. Because the timer tick has higher priority than the receive interrupt, a tick that arrives mid-write sees the odd counter, discards the torn read in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time without spinning, and keeps executing the active chunk for as long as its lease and evidence remain valid. A crashed or stalled application processor cannot leave the counter odd, because it never writes the slot. Its failure appears only as an absence of incoming frames, and the active chunk's lease expires on schedule.

Formally, the reader validates the snapshot using two boundary counter observations\index{Sequence lock!shared memory}:
$$\ReadStartSequenceCount \equiv \ReadEndSequenceCount \equiv 0 \pmod 2 \quad \text{and} \quad \ReadStartSequenceCount = \ReadEndSequenceCount,$$
where an odd count signals an active write and a value mismatch signals preemption during the copy. Unlike mutexes or semaphores, this protocol never suspends either participant. Because the reader never retries within a single tick, its computational overhead remains strictly $\mathcal{O}(1)$ regardless of writer activity. Correct execution requires that memory loads occur in strict programmatic order. Within a single core arbitrating between an interrupt handler and the periodic tick, compiler optimization barriers prevent instruction reordering. However, when a DMA engine or a second processor core writes the slot directly, hardware memory barriers become mandatory. On Arm Cortex-M profile cores, this requires the full-system data memory barrier instruction (`DMB`) [@arm2012an321]. Omitting this barrier allows out-of-order execution pipelines to speculatively load payload fields before validating the sequence counter, silently allowing torn data into the control loop.

A **wait-free three-slot mailbox**[^fn-wait-free-mailbox] can avoid read/write collisions by assigning separate slots to the writer, the published proposal, and the reader. Atomic publication transfers slot ownership; it must never let the writer overwrite the reader's active slot. Unlike the one-attempt seqlock, this design can provide a complete published snapshot without discarding a collided read. Its extra storage and ownership protocol must still be checked on the target hardware. Simpson's four-slot mechanism reaches the same guarantee, a complete snapshot for a reader that never waits, using only single-bit control variables written with ordinary stores and no atomic read-modify-write instruction [@simpson1990four]. Neither design makes an old proposal fresh or extends its lease.

[^fn-wait-free-mailbox]: **Wait-Free**: @herlihy1991waitfree defined an implementation as wait-free when every operation finishes in a bounded number of its own steps, whatever the other processes do. That is stronger than lock-free progress, which guarantees only that some operation completes while a particular one may retry indefinitely. The one-attempt seqlock read is bounded but can come back empty-handed; the slot mailbox is bounded and always returns a complete snapshot, and the extra slot is the price of that second property. \index{Wait-free synchronization!slot mailbox}

Sequential diagnostic telemetry, by contrast, operates under event semantics. A single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) ring buffer preserves an ordered log of events until its bounded capacity fills, whereas the proposal mailbox exposes only the latest complete candidate state. The permission interface relies on these bounded-access guarantees to eliminate wait states; it intentionally discards historical command queues.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The memory-ordering primitives, cache-line padding, and slot-ownership protocols that implement both exchanges are developed in @sec-appendix-systems-ipc.
:::

No robotics middleware setting can stand in for the chunk lease, because none derives its parameters from the physical stopping budget and none executes on the consumer's own hardware clock at the point of actuation. Middleware can still approximate the mailbox's state-message semantics, and the mapping shows how far configuration goes. In ROS 2, communication relies on the Data Distribution Service (DDS) or equivalent publish-subscribe transports [@macenski2022robot], whose Quality-of-Service (QoS) policies reflect real-time contracts only partially [@omg2015dds]. Configuring a *keep-last* history depth of one provides state-message semantics by retaining only the freshest sample. Selecting *best-effort* reliability drops lost packets rather than triggering retransmissions, avoiding the burst of stale samples that *reliable* delivery releases after network blips. A DDS *deadline* policy raises notification events when sample inter-arrival times exceed a threshold, acting as an alerting heartbeat without enforcing authority revocation. Similarly, a DDS *lifespan* policy purges samples whose age exceeds a configured threshold, but this mechanism relies on synchronized network clocks, defaults to arrival timestamps when synchronization degrades, and controls only message transport rather than granted actuation authority. Callback scheduling within middleware executors also introduces variable dispatch jitter, requiring dedicated response-time analyses across end-to-end processing chains [@casini2019response]. At the direct hardware interface, the ros2_control framework implements a nonblocking realtime buffer using a single try-lock attempt: if the writer holds the mutex, the read aborts and the controller retains its prior command [@rostools2025realtime], mimicking the one-attempt semantics of a seqlock. Regardless of middleware abstractions, the physical permission path must independently enforce its own freshness checks and lease bounds.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The inverse failure, middleware that reports healthy delivery while transmitting stale payload data, is developed in @sec-memory-failure-modes.
:::

Because the receive interrupt write routine is brief and resumes immediately after the tick completes, an access collision discards at most one read attempt without delaying the tick. However, if the upstream link halts completely, the mailbox slot remains unchanged across thousands of consecutive ticks. Bounded reader execution time does not guarantee bounded publication latency. The system therefore requires an explicit physical policy governing how long a previously admitted motion chunk may continue commanding actuators. Under the first law, irreversibility (principle \ref{pri-vol4-irreversibility}), every millisecond that a stalled proposal retains actuation authority produces physical displacement that cannot be retracted. That exposure has to be priced against the stopping budget, which makes the length of a proposal's authority the next design decision.

## Chunk Lease Sizing from the Stopping Budget {#sec-nervous-lease-sizing}

A learned policy runtime can stall for many reasons: a page fault, thermal throttling on the vision accelerator, memory fragmentation, or an uncaught exception in perception preprocessing. The robot does not stop when its software does. A loaded base keeps its momentum ($\LinearMomentum = \Mass \SpeedAtDetection$) and covers `{python} TickDelayBudget.mm_per_ms_str` every millisecond at the drive limit, while the downstream controller keeps converting the remaining waypoints of the last admitted chunk into setpoints. To keep an unrenewed chunk from driving the machine into an obstacle, the permission path must end that chunk's authority on its own hardware clock, whether or not the proposer ever reports its failure. How long it should wait before doing so is a question about distance, not software.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-machine-lease-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHUNK LEASE AGAINST THE STOPPING BUDGET (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease, the three-timer paragraph,
# │          the overrun paragraph, @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation,
# │          the H4 paragraph, and the summary takeaways.
# │ Goal:    Add the lease path (stopping-budget row 4) to the running total
# │          that @sec-body-kinetic-momentum left, and state the pre-brake
# │          ceiling the lease must fit inside.
# │ Show:    ceiling 258.3 ms; row 4 = 93.0 mm; running total 742.5 -> 835.5 mm;
# │          renewal-to-onset 82 ms; 176.3 ms of ceiling left; renewal
# │          floor 50 + 5 = 55 ms below the 60 ms lease.
# │ How:     calc_watchdog_lease_bound on D_clear less the fixed overheads;
# │          every term from RM / AISLE (canon §3.2-§3.4).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, fmt_display_math, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class MachineLeaseBudget:
    """Chunk lease sized from the mobile manipulator's stopping budget at its drive limit."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (loaded, dry floor)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen (1 kHz permission loop)
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative (EtherCAT cycle)
    f_heartbeat = AISLE.heartbeat_rate  # category: chosen
    t_heartbeat_timeout = AISLE.heartbeat_timeout  # category: chosen
    t_self_watchdog = AISLE.mcu_self_watchdog  # category: chosen
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen (chunk-policy renewal rate)
    t_renewal_jitter = 5 * millisecond  # category: chosen (renewal-jitter allowance; scenario assumption)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    overhead = (delta_loc + delta_margin).to(millimeter)
    ceiling = calc_watchdog_lease_bound(
        clearance_distance=d_clear - delta_loc - delta_margin,
        initial_velocity=v,
        max_deceleration=a_brake,
    )
    d_brake = ceiling["d_brake"].to(millimeter)
    t_ceiling = ceiling["t_total_delay_max"].to(millisecond)  # whole pre-brake delay, onset included
    d_onset = (v * t_act).to(millimeter)
    prior_total = (d_brake + overhead + d_onset).to(millimeter)  # rows 1-3 (@sec-body-kinetic-momentum)
    t_lease_path = (t_lease + t_tick + t_bus).to(millisecond)
    d_lease_path = (v * t_lease_path).to(millimeter)  # row 4
    running_total = (prior_total + d_lease_path).to(millimeter)
    remaining = (d_clear - running_total).to(millimeter)
    t_renewal_to_onset = (t_lease_path + t_act).to(millisecond)
    t_ceiling_left = (t_ceiling - t_renewal_to_onset).to(millisecond)
    mm_per_ms = (v * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)
    t_chunk_period = (1 / f_chunk).to(millisecond)
    t_renewal_need = (t_chunk_period + t_renewal_jitter).to(millisecond)  # lease lower limit

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_ceiling.magnitude - 258.333) < 5e-3, f"Pre-brake ceiling drifted: {t_ceiling}")
    check(abs(d_brake.magnitude - 562.5) < 1e-6, f"Braking row drifted: {d_brake}")
    check(abs(prior_total.magnitude - 742.5) < 1e-6, f"Rows 1-3 total drifted: {prior_total}")
    check(abs(t_lease_path.magnitude - 62.0) < 1e-6, f"Lease path drifted: {t_lease_path}")
    check(abs(d_lease_path.magnitude - 93.0) < 1e-6, f"Row 4 drifted: {d_lease_path}")
    check(abs(running_total.magnitude - 835.5) < 1e-6, f"Running total drifted: {running_total}")
    check(abs(remaining.magnitude - 264.5) < 1e-6, f"Remaining clear distance drifted: {remaining}")
    check(abs(t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-6, f"Renewal-to-onset drifted: {t_renewal_to_onset}")
    check(
        abs((remaining / v).to(millisecond).magnitude - t_ceiling_left.magnitude) < 1e-6,
        "Time left in the ceiling must equal the remaining distance at the drive limit",
    )
    check(abs(t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk lease drifted: {t_lease}")
    check(abs(f_heartbeat.to(hertz).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, f"Heartbeat rate drifted: {f_heartbeat}")
    check(abs(t_heartbeat_timeout.to(millisecond).magnitude - 30.0) < 1e-9, f"Heartbeat timeout drifted: {t_heartbeat_timeout}")
    check(abs(t_self_watchdog.to(millisecond).magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, f"Self-watchdog timeout drifted: {t_self_watchdog}")
    check(abs(t_chunk_period.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-6, f"Chunk period drifted: {t_chunk_period}")
    check(abs(t_renewal_need.magnitude - 55.0) < 1e-6, f"Lease lower limit drifted: {t_renewal_need}")
    check(t_renewal_need < t_lease, "Lease rule: chunk period plus jitter must be shorter than the lease")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    d_onset_str = fmt_length(d_onset, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    prior_total_str = fmt_length(prior_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(t_ceiling, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_lease_path_str = fmt_length(d_lease_path, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    running_total_str = fmt_length(running_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_ceiling_left_str = fmt_latency(t_ceiling_left, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    mm_per_ms_str = fmt_length(mm_per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    f_heartbeat_str = fmt_frequency(f_heartbeat, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_heartbeat_timeout_str = fmt_latency(t_heartbeat_timeout, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_self_watchdog_str = fmt_latency(t_self_watchdog, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_jitter_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_jitter, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_need_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_need, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_margin_str = fmt_length(delta_margin, unit=millimeter, precision=0)

    _v = fmt(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    _a = fmt(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    _clear = fmt(d_clear, unit=millimeter, precision=0, commas=False)
    _over = fmt(overhead, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    _brake = fmt(d_brake, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _ceil = fmt(t_ceiling, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    _lease = fmt(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _tick = fmt(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _bus = fmt(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _act = fmt(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _path = fmt(t_lease_path, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _row4 = fmt(d_lease_path, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    _prior = fmt(prior_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _run = fmt(running_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _rem = fmt(remaining, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _onset = fmt(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _left = fmt(t_ceiling_left, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    _period = fmt(t_chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _jit = fmt(t_renewal_jitter, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    _need = fmt(t_renewal_need, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    brake_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\frac{{v^2}}{{2a_{{\text{{brake}}}}}} = \frac{{({_v}\ \text{{m/s}})^2}}{{2 \times {_a}\ \text{{m/s}}^2}} = {_brake}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    ceiling_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} \le \frac{{{_clear} - {_over} - {_brake}\ \text{{mm}}}}{{{_v}\ \text{{m/s}}}} = {_ceil}\ \text{{ms}}"
    )
    row4_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"v\,(T_{{\text{{lease}}}} + T_{{\text{{tick}}}} + T_{{\text{{bus}}}}) = {_v}\ \text{{m/s}} \times ({_lease} + {_tick} + {_bus})\ \text{{ms}} = {_row4}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    total_math = fmt_display_math(rf"{_prior} + {_row4} = {_run}\ \text{{mm}}, \quad {_clear} - {_run} = {_rem}\ \text{{mm}}")
    time_math = fmt_display_math(rf"{_path} + {_act} = {_onset}\ \text{{ms}}, \quad {_ceil} - {_onset} = {_left}\ \text{{ms}}")
    floor_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"T_{{\text{{chunk}}}} + T_{{\text{{jitter}}}} = {_period} + {_jit} = {_need}\ \text{{ms}} < T_{{\text{{lease}}}} = {_lease}\ \text{{ms}}"
    )
```

::: {#dfn-nervous-chunk-lease .callout-definition title="Chunk lease"}

***Chunk lease***\index{Chunk lease!definition}\index{Lease!stopping budget} is the interval, counted on the permission path's own clock from a chunk's admission, during which that admitted chunk may keep driving the actuators without a successful replacement; when it expires, the permission path ends the chunk's authority and commands the state-matched fallback, a stop profile chosen from the machine's measured speed and pose.

1.  **Significance**: The lease enters the pre-brake delay $\PrebrakeDelay$ of the stopping budget, so each millisecond of it costs $\SpeedAtDetection$ of clear distance, `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.mm_per_ms_str` at the running machine's drive limit. The machine's `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str` lease, with the tick and bus cycle that detect and deliver its expiry, adds `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.d_lease_path_str` to the stopping budget (notebook \ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}).
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a heartbeat timeout, which shows only that the host is alive, a lease is renewed only by a freshly admitted proposal, and its length is derived from the plant rather than configured: above the proposer's renewal floor and below the stopping budget's ceiling. Unlike an evidence deadline, it bounds how long one motion segment may execute, not how long the observation behind it stays valid.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Lengthening the lease to ride out proposer hiccups. A longer lease buys continuity with clearance, and a lease that reaches the pre-brake ceiling commits the machine to motion it can no longer stop in time.

:::

In classical distributed systems, a lease grants bounded access to a shared digital resource, such as a distributed lock or cache entry, expiring automatically if the leaseholder crashes [@gray1989leases]. In physical AI, the leased resource is the kinetic authority to move mass through space. Because physical motion cannot be undone, the duration of a lease must be formally derived from the physical stopping budget. The distance covered during the lease, the detection latency, the fieldbus transit, and the brake onset, together with the braking distance itself, must fit within the available clearance $\ClearDistance$ after the localization uncertainty and protective margin are subtracted. Rearranging the stopping-distance relation of @eq-body-stopping-distance, $\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay + \SpeedAtDetection^2/2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration + \LocalizationBound + \ProtectiveClearanceMargin \le \ClearDistance$, and dividing the remaining pre-braking distance by vehicle velocity yields the **pre-brake ceiling**\index{Pre-brake ceiling}, representing the maximum tolerable delay $\PrebrakeDelay$ before physical braking deceleration must commence:
$$\PrebrakeDelay \le \frac{\ClearDistance - \LocalizationBound - \ProtectiveClearanceMargin - \SpeedAtDetection^2/2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration}{\SpeedAtDetection}$$ {#eq-nervous-prebrake}
where $\SpeedAtDetection$ represents operating velocity, $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$ denotes verified braking deceleration, and $\LocalizationBound$ and $\ProtectiveClearanceMargin$ represent the localization uncertainty and safety clearance of that formulation. As operating speed $\SpeedAtDetection$ decreases, the required braking distance shrinks quadratically while the velocity divisor decreases linearly, causing the pre-brake ceiling to expand toward infinity at rest. At maximum operating speed, however, every millisecond allocated to the lease path consumes exactly $\SpeedAtDetection$ units of stopping clearance.

Panel (a) of @fig-04-multirate-cadence-buffer draws the lease on the running machine's own clocks. The chunk policy renews twice and then stalls; the tick keeps executing the last admitted chunk only until the lease counted from that admission lapses, and the next tick, one bus cycle, and the brake onset then bring the fallback stop. Notebook \ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease} evaluates @eq-nervous-prebrake for the mobile manipulator at its drive limit and prices that sequence inside it.

::: {#nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease .callout-notebook title="The price of a lease"}

**Problem**: In the illustrative aisle scenario, the warehouse mobile manipulator cruises at its drive limit toward a person who has stepped out from a rack end and stopped. The permission path admits one last chunk and then receives no admissible replacement. How much time remains before braking must begin, and how much of it, and of the clear distance, does the chunk lease spend?

**Variables**:

* Speed $\SpeedAtDetection =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.v_str`, the drive limit (illustrative); braking deceleration $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.a_brake_str`, loaded on a dry floor (illustrative).
* Clear distance $\ClearDistance =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.d_clear_str` (illustrative), less localization error $\LocalizationBound =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.delta_loc_str` (illustrative) and protective clearance $\ProtectiveClearanceMargin =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.delta_margin_str` (chosen).
* Brake onset $\ActuatorResponseTime =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_act_str` (illustrative); permission tick $\PermissionLoopPeriod =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_tick_str` (chosen); bus cycle $\CommandTransportTime =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_bus_str` (illustrative).
* Chunk lease $\ChunkLease =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str`; renewal period $\ChunkRenewalPeriod =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_chunk_period_str` with a `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_renewal_jitter_str` variation allowance $\RenewalJitterAllowance$ (all chosen).

**Math**: The braking term and the ceiling of @eq-nervous-prebrake:
`{python} MachineLeaseBudget.brake_math`
`{python} MachineLeaseBudget.ceiling_math`
The stopping-budget terms that @sec-body-kinetic-momentum already charged (braking, the localization and clearance overheads, and onset travel $\SpeedAtDetection\,\ActuatorResponseTime =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.d_onset_str`) hold `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.prior_total_str` of the clear distance. The lease path, lease plus the tick that notices its expiry plus the bus cycle that delivers the stop, is the next term:
`{python} MachineLeaseBudget.row4_math`
`{python} MachineLeaseBudget.total_math`
In time, from the last admission to brake onset, and against the ceiling:
`{python} MachineLeaseBudget.time_math`
Continuous tracking also sets a floor under the lease:
`{python} MachineLeaseBudget.floor_math`

**Systems insight**: A chunk lease is a term in the stopping budget, not a timeout chosen for convenience. Each millisecond added to it costs `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.mm_per_ms_str` of clear distance at the drive limit, distance that the observation age and the stop profile still need, so the lease sits just above its renewal floor rather than anywhere under the ceiling.

:::

The renewal floor is the lease duration needed to cover the budgeted inter-arrival interval between successful admissions without starving trajectory execution. Because this floor cannot rely solely on the model's 99th-percentile ($\text{p99}$) inference latency, it must accommodate bus transit, validation overhead, and mailbox synchronization jitter. If a renewal fails to arrive before the lease expires, the system terminates trajectory tracking rather than granting an unearned extension. The `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling_left_str` remaining under the pre-brake ceiling is not spare margin either. It must still absorb the observation's age at admission, which @sec-nervous-coupled-budget charges against it, and the jerk limits of the braking profile.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-event-timing
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE CAPTURE-TO-BRAKE-ONSET EVENT TIMING (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-04-event-timing in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing; the table
# │          that @sec-body-latency-pipeline, @sec-perception-latency-waterfall,
# │          @sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff, and @sec-placement-isolation-decisions
# │          point to.
# │ Goal:    Name the four events once and show every interval between them from
# │          its one registry owner, so no chapter keeps its own stage list.
# │ Show:    capture -> dispatch 51.6 ms; dispatch -> admission 63.3 ms;
# │          L = 114.9 ms; admission -> brake onset 82 ms; capture -> brake
# │          onset 196.9 ms (= tau_delay 133.6 + Delta_da 63.3).
# │ How:     AISLE.perception_age, AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission,
# │          AISLE.t_capture_to_admission, AISLE.t_admission_to_brake_onset,
# │          AISLE.t_capture_to_brake_onset (MLSysIM).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class CaptureToBrakeTiming:
    """Three intervals between four events, each from its one registry owner."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # category: derived (capture to dispatch)
    t_da = AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission.to(millisecond)  # category: derived (allocation; dispatch to admission)
    t_resp = AISLE.t_admission_to_brake_onset.to(millisecond)  # category: derived (lease, tick, bus, onset)
    t_validate = AISLE.t_plan_validate.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (inside t_da)
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay.to(millisecond)  # category: derived (the pre-brake delay, without t_da)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_replace = AISLE.t_capture_to_admission.to(millisecond)  # replacement latency L
    t_total = AISLE.t_capture_to_brake_onset.to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_age.magnitude - 51.6) < 1e-9, f"Capture-to-dispatch age drifted: {t_age}")
    check(abs(t_da.magnitude - 63.31072) < 1e-6, f"Dispatch-to-admission allocation drifted: {t_da}")
    check(abs((t_age + t_da - t_replace).magnitude) < 1e-9, "L must be the sum of the first two intervals.")
    check(abs(t_resp.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, f"Admission-to-onset response drifted: {t_resp}")
    check(abs((t_replace + t_resp - t_total).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The three intervals must close on the total.")
    check(abs((tau_delay + t_da - t_total).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The pre-brake delay plus Delta_da must equal the total.")
    check(t_validate < t_da, "Validation is counted once, inside Delta_da.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_da_str = fmt_latency(t_da, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_replace_str = fmt_latency(t_replace, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_resp_str = fmt_latency(t_resp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_total_str = fmt_latency(t_total, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Every charge in this budget is an interval between the four boundary events introduced in @sec-body-latency-pipeline\index{Capture!event}. *Capture* dates an observation at its exposure midpoint, *dispatch* hands that evidence to the proposer, *admission* accepts a chunk built on it and starts the chunk's lease, and *brake onset* marks the first physical braking force at the drives. Between these four events lie three intervals, each derived in exactly one chapter (@tbl-04-event-timing). Only row 3, the stalled-proposer response, is derived here, from the lease notebook. Rows 1 and 2 enter Part I as allocations: the observation age that @sec-perception-latency-waterfall will build stage by stage, and the dispatch-to-admission interval that @sec-placement-dispatch-admission will charge to the board link and the validator. Later chapters charge time against these events and this table rather than keeping their own stage lists.

| Interval                                                  | Opens at  | Closes at   | What it contains                                                                                                             |                                        Allocation | Derived in                        |
|:----------------------------------------------------------|:----------|:------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------:|:----------------------------------|
| **1.** Observation age $\ObservationAge$                  | capture   | dispatch    | Half the exposure, readout, transport, DMA, image signal processing, perception backbone, hand-off to the proposer           |         `{python} CaptureToBrakeTiming.t_age_str` | @sec-perception-latency-waterfall |
| **2.** Dispatch to admission $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ | dispatch  | admission   | Proposer inference (charged in full), board link, deserialization, whole-plan validation, activation, wait for the next tick |          `{python} CaptureToBrakeTiming.t_da_str` | @sec-placement-dispatch-admission |
| **1 + 2.** Replacement latency $\Latency$                 | capture   | admission   | Rows 1 and 2; validation is counted once, inside row 2                                                                       | **`{python} CaptureToBrakeTiming.t_replace_str`** | @sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff    |
| **3.** Stalled-proposer response                          | admission | brake onset | Chunk lease, one permission tick, one fieldbus cycle, brake onset                                                            |        `{python} CaptureToBrakeTiming.t_resp_str` | @sec-nervous-lease-sizing         |
| **1 + 2 + 3.** Capture to brake onset                     | capture   | brake onset | All three intervals                                                                                                          |   **`{python} CaptureToBrakeTiming.t_total_str`** | @sec-enforcement-composite-budget |

: **The capture-to-brake-onset timing budget of the running machine**: Four events bound three intervals, and each interval is derived in one chapter. Rows 1 and 3 together form the `{python} CaptureToBrakeTiming.tau_delay_str` pre-brake delay of the stopping budget; row 2 is the allocation that budget must still pay for. Row 2 charges the whole inference after dispatch, although its vision stage already lies in row 1, so the sum is conservative. Every value is an allocation or an illustrative stage time to qualify on the loaded machine, not a measurement. {#tbl-04-event-timing tbl-colwidths="[20,9,9,34,12,16]"}

The table also shows why the stopping budget and the lease rule charge different ages. The stopping budget's pre-brake delay sums rows 1 and 3 and leaves row 2 to be paid from the spare that the elementary budget of @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline left, because row 2's length depends on where the proposer and the permission path run, a decision @sec-placement-dispatch-admission makes. A renewal cannot defer that payment. A replacement chunk spends row 2 before its lease even starts, so the evidence age that the lease rule of @sec-nervous-coupled-budget charges at admission is rows 1 and 2 together.

### Supervisory timers and proposal wire contracts {#sec-nervous-supervisory-timers}

Granting a fresh lease at admission without charging the time the observation already spent in inference and board-link transit, or waiting on a single timeout while a hung policy thread sits inside a live host kernel, lets the drives keep tracking a trajectory whose sensory evidence is already stale or whose producer has stopped updating. Evidence keeps aging from capture onward, and admitting a chunk starts its lease on the microcontroller's clock without rolling that age back; because neither the dispatch timestamp nor the newly granted lease accounts for the dispatch-to-admission interval, the evidence-age check must charge row 2 of @tbl-04-event-timing explicitly. Authority over an admitted chunk then ends at the earliest of four events: its evidence freshness deadline passes, its lease expires without a successful replacement, the host heartbeat times out, or an independent safety reflex such as the protective scanner path detects an obstacle. None of these waits for the others, and which fires first depends on the scene. At the conveyor, the tracked evidence horizon that @sec-brain-two-proposers computed is several times longer than the lease, so there a stalled chunk loses its authority to the lease. The chunk lease bounds how long one admitted motion segment may execute. How long the strategic goal stays meaningful is a separate grant, the intent lease of @sec-intent-lease, and neither is the nominal planning horizon.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The freshness deadline that bounds how old evidence may be at actuation is established in @sec-body-measurement-freshness.
:::

Three independent supervisory timers guard the exchange, and each monitors a distinct failure domain:

1. **The chunk lease ($\ChunkLease =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str`):** Bounds how long an admitted proposal may command actuators. Only a freshly validated, admitted proposal chunk renews the lease. Its duration is derived directly from the physical stopping budget, sitting between the renewal floor and the pre-brake ceiling (notebook \ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}).
2. **The host heartbeat ($\HostHeartbeatRate =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.f_heartbeat_str`, timeout `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_heartbeat_timeout_str`):** Asserts that the application processor operating system kernel and user-space runtime remain alive. Expiry of this timeout revokes the active proposal without waiting for the chunk lease. Heartbeat pulses **never renew the chunk lease**, because a live process can easily suffer algorithmic livelock or produce corrupted, out-of-distribution setpoints.
3. **The microcontroller self-watchdog ($\SelfWatchdogTimeout =$ `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_self_watchdog_str`):** Monitors whether the permission path completes its required checks within the watchdog interval. The permission loop feeds this hardware watchdog only upon successfully completing all verification checks in a tick; a hung enforcer trips the watchdog even if timer interrupts continue firing (@sec-nervous-fallacies-pitfalls).

A watchdog refresh confirms only that the specific task servicing the timer is still executing. In *Bookout v. Toyota* (2013), litigation centered on whether a timer-tick interrupt could continue petting a watchdog while application-level control tasks had hung [@barr2013toyota]. Although federal investigations by NASA and NHTSA identified no electronic mechanism capable of causing large unintended accelerations [@nasa2011toyota], the dispute highlights an essential real-time principle: watchdog refresh points must be coupled to the completion of safety-critical algorithmic cycles rather than independent periodic interrupts.

Real-time safety requires wrapping the proposer's payload in a transport and authority envelope. The system enforces chunk leases through the **proposal header**\index{Proposal header}, a structured wire contract that enables the permission path to validate candidate trajectories without placing trust in host application software. The header encapsulates a monotonically increasing sequence number, the evidence timestamp of the source sensory frame (including clock conversion error bounds), the host dispatch timestamp, the requested lease duration (which the permission path caps at the lease it derives, so a proposer can ask for less authority but never more), a cryptographic parent-record digest for provenance tracking, the coordinate frame identifier, the payload type enum, and a 32-bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC-32). For the default payload type the payload consists of $\ActionChunkHorizon$ kinematic waypoints specifying joint coordinates and velocities; the payload-type field is where other command forms announce themselves, so an impedance target (@sec-nervous-command-interface) carries its stiffness and damping gains beside its equilibrium waypoints. In this layered architecture, the learned policy expresses kinematic intent, the permission enforcer converts admitted waypoints into position setpoints, and the drives regulate joint velocity and motor current. The payload deliberately omits raw torque commands; while direct-torque policies require alternate wire representations and specialized admission checks, their outputs remain untrusted proposals. In all cases, an admitted proposal retains execution authority only until the earlier of its lease expiration and its evidence freshness deadline, regardless of whether cancellation packets arrive across the network.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The proposal payload, the candidate motion and the evidence times it carries, is established in @sec-brain-proposer-information.
:::

Industrial safety networking adopted the same transport safeguards decades before the advent of learned robotic proposers. Functional-safety fieldbus standards such as IEC 61784-3 establish the **black-channel principle**\index{Black-channel principle}: transmission media, network controllers, and intermediate switches are treated as untrusted, fallible channels, requiring safety-critical packets to encapsulate self-contained integrity and timing protections verified exclusively at communication endpoints [@iec61784-3-2021]. Fieldbus profiles like PROFIsafe and Safety over EtherCAT (FSoE) exemplify this architecture. FSoE protects frames against corruption using CRCs, against repetition and packet loss using sequence counters, against misrouting using unique connection identifiers, and against transit delay using watchdog timers; missing or delayed frames force the receiver into a deterministic safe state [@etg2019fsoe]. The proposal header mirrors this design field for field: checksums guard integrity, sequence numbers detect drops, payload identifiers ensure proper dispatch, and the chunk lease replaces the watchdog timer. The physical link between host application processor and safety microcontroller operates as an untrusted black channel; end-to-end header checks allow the permission path to enforce its declared physical admission contract without trusting host operating system integrity. Classical real-time theory provides the complementary semantic foundation. Kopetz defines a computing system's internal representation of a dynamic physical entity as a *real-time image*, which remains *temporally accurate*\index{Temporal accuracy} only during a bounded physical duration following the initial observation [@kopetz2011real]. The proposal's evidence deadline represents this temporal accuracy window applied to sensory inputs, while the chunk lease bounds the duration of derived actuation. This architecture adds one thing to these precedents, the grounding of temporal validity. Whereas industrial fieldbuses configure watchdog timeouts empirically and real-time images reflect passive plant dynamics, the chunk lease is derived analytically from the physical stopping budget above and the proposer's renewal floor below (@eq-nervous-prebrake, notebook \ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Byte layout:** The proposal header's and chunk payload's fields, types, and offsets are given in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-header.
:::

Every record crossing the proposal boundary expresses temporal quantities referenced to the safety microcontroller's monotonic clock. Upstream producers operating on independent oscillator domains map timestamps using a versioned affine transformation and transmit explicit synchronization error bounds, which the safety consumer adds to all age evaluations. Wall-clock calendar time is restricted to diagnostic logging and software release expiration; it never enters real-time safety gating.

Individual boundary records guard against three orthogonal failure modes through three distinct mechanisms, only two of them cryptographic. A checksum across the header and payload, a CRC rather than a cryptographic function, detects transmission bit flips and memory corruption during transit, leaving origin authentication unaddressed. Similarly, a cryptographic digest of the parent record establishes computational lineage without authenticating the sender. Cryptographic message authentication codes (MACs) appear exclusively where sender identity conveys explicit operational authority: network teleoperation commands, immutable authority audit logs, and release artifacts verified during deployment. Learned model proposals omit cryptographic signatures entirely, because the permission enforcer validates candidates based on physical admissibility and temporal freshness rather than origin. A cryptographic key stored inside an untrusted host environment provides no assurance of kinematic safety.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How a teleoperation command's authentication tag is verified and priced against the fallback deadline is developed in @sec-intervention-authenticating-intervention.
:::

The reader's possible failures fall into four classes (@tbl-04-boundary-fallbacks), and none of them lets a failed producer make the permission path wait. The classes keep the exchange from blocking; they do not by themselves contain the plant, because the fallback each one selects still needs bounded timing and a validated stop, and even a valid admitted chunk still has to be stepped from the proposer's coarse waypoint spacing down to the permission tick's rate.

| Failure Class        | Reader Detection Condition                                       | Physical Systems Fallback Action                                        | Bounded Response                      |
|:---------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------|
| **Torn / In-Flight** | Odd $\ReadStartSequenceCount$ or changed $\ReadEndSequenceCount$ | Reject current snapshot; use admissible prior chunk or fallback         | One bounded attempt; measure duration |
| **Malformed**        | Checksum or configured command bound fails                       | Reject candidate; retain admissible active chunk or use fallback        | Measure check and response            |
| **Stale**            | Past proposal expiry or evidence deadline (local clock)          | Reject stale candidate; end active authority if its own deadline passed | Deadline from plant budget            |
| **Missing**          | Sequence gap                                                     | Record audit gap; evaluate current record on its own merits             | One tick for flag                     |

: **Boundary contract failure classes and deterministic fallback matrix**: Exchange faults across the proposal boundary by class, with the fallback each selects. Fallback paths are selected without waiting on host recovery. {#tbl-04-boundary-fallbacks tbl-colwidths="[20,30,35,15]"}

### Rate interpolation and boundary fallback execution {#sec-nervous-rate-interpolation}

Holding each admitted waypoint constant for its full `{python} MachineTiers.chunk_step_str` spacing until the next waypoint arrives injects staircase position steps into the drives rather than a smooth trajectory, delaying reference tracking by half the step spacing on average and exciting high-frequency structural resonances. Bridging the learned policy's renewal rate (`{python} MachineTiers.f_chunk_str`) and the real-time permission tick (`{python} TickDelayBudget.t_tick_str`) without those disturbances requires guarding against three sampled-data failure modes: reference lag, spectral aliasing, and buffer starvation. Because the zero-order hold's latency sits entirely on the feedforward reference path outside the feedback loop, it appears as tracking error rather than eroding feedback phase margins (@sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag), and confusing reference lag with closed-loop phase lag often leads engineers to misdiagnose tracking errors as plant instability. To eliminate discrete steps across chunk boundaries, the permission enforcer constructs a quintic Hermite spline bridge matching boundary position, velocity, and acceleration. These six boundary constraints guarantee $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ continuity across chunk transitions, meaning position, velocity, and acceleration all stay continuous. Evaluating this admitted spline at `{python} MachineTiers.f_perm_str` yields continuous position references, smooth velocity feeds, and feedforward acceleration profiles for the underlying joint controllers.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Action chunking, which produces the trajectory segments this interpolator densifies, is established in @sec-brain-action-chunking.
:::

Spectral aliasing occurs when unmodeled high-frequency mechanical vibration or sensor noise, sampled too slowly, reappears as a false low-frequency signal in the slower streams that estimators and the tick consume. The architecture mitigates aliasing through front-end analog filtering followed by multi-rate digital decimation,[^fn-fir-smoothing-delay] low-pass filtering a fast sample stream before keeping only one sample in several, within the high-rate microcontroller domain. Classical sampled-data control models assume constant, deterministic sampling periods. Temporal jitter, a sampling interval that varies from cycle to cycle, degrades phase margin more severely than a constant delay of equivalent mean duration [@cervin2003control]. Discrete trajectory execution also assumes setpoints replenish continuously before downstream buffers drain. The permission path enforces these invariants via cycle-deterministic hardware timer interrupts and real-time buffer-depth accounting. If the upstream planner stalls and the trajectory buffer reaches its terminal waypoint, the enforcer rejects stale extrapolation and commands a validated local stopping profile.

[^fn-fir-smoothing-delay]: **Filter Group Delay**: Digital smoothing filters commonly applied in machine learning pipelines introduce significant phase lag when placed inside feedback control loops. An $\FilterTapCount$-tap moving-average finite impulse response (FIR) filter imposes an average group delay of $(\FilterTapCount-1)/2$ sample intervals. Consequently, a `{python} TickDelayBudget.n_fir_str`-tap moving average operating at the `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_tick_str` permission tick delays feedback signals by `{python} TickDelayBudget.tau_fir_str`. At the illustrative `{python} TickDelayBudget.f_c_str` crossover frequency from @sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag, this delay burns `{python} TickDelayBudget.phi_fir_str`$^\circ$ of phase, `{python} TickDelayBudget.fir_over_mult_str` the design allowance. In real-time control paths, decimation and filter topologies must be selected for minimal phase lag rather than cosmetic smoothing. \index{Finite impulse response filter!group delay}

An overrun costs something different at each of the four tiers:

* **Current loop (`{python} MachineTiers.f_current_str`):** Its jitter allowance is below $10\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ (@tbl-04-synthesis-grid). A timing overrun, gate-drive desynchronization, or current spike trips a hardware fault line that disables the inverter's PWM stages.
* **Permission tick (`{python} MachineTiers.f_perm_str`):** A deadline overrun by the enforcer software sends the machine to the local deceleration stop.
* **Chunk policy (`{python} MachineTiers.f_chunk_str`):** Inference latency is stochastic (`{python} MachineStallTravel.t_chunk_str` at p99), so some chunks arrive late. A late chunk costs nothing until the active chunk's lease or evidence deadline runs out, and the enforcer never waits on the proposer's optimistic estimate of when it will finish. When either deadline passes, the enforcer commands the state-matched fallback.
* **Intent planner (`{python} MachineTiers.f_intent_str`):** Its goals expire under a separate *intent lease*, a longer grant of authority over the goal itself rather than over any motion (developed in @sec-intent-lease). When it lapses, the system holds station instead of chasing a stale goal.

The lease notebook charged the tick and the bus cycle as fixed terms, `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_tick_str` and `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_bus_str`, as though each were certain to finish on time. That premise is the next thing to establish. It requires a worst-case response bound for every stage between the mailbox and the drives, and no benchmark or faster processor substitutes for one.

## Real-Time Command Transport and Bus Determinism {#sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses}

A profiling campaign can run the permission tick for days without a missed deadline and still not establish the tick's worst case. An empirical percentile says how often sampled executions stayed under a threshold; it says nothing about executions that meet a combination of competing tasks, memory contention, or peripheral delay the campaign never produced. The lease budget needs the other kind of number: a response-time bound that accounts for every unit of permitted computation and queuing delay along the critical path under defined operating conditions. In an embodied system, timing determinism protects both stability and safety, because delayed feedback erodes the controller's phase margin and delayed actuation consumes stopping clearance before the chassis can decelerate. Bounding the tick on the microcontroller comes first; bounding the drive network that carries its admitted setpoints to the motors follows the same logic [@kopetz2011real].

### Response time analysis and execution variance {#sec-nervous-rta-variance}

A permission tick whose own instructions finish in `{python} TickVocabulary.t_wcet_str` can still miss its `{python} TickVocabulary.t_deadline_str` deadline if a lower-priority link driver masks interrupts while re-arming a DMA descriptor or a burst of higher-priority timer interrupts preempts the tick mid-cycle. Response Time Analysis (RTA) bounds a task's total response time by summing the three constituents introduced in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning: execution time, blocking delay, and preemption interference [@joseph1986finding; @audsley1993applying]. To guarantee schedulability, each term requires an analytical upper bound under specified operating conditions:
$$\WorstCaseResponseTime_i = \WorstCaseExecutionTime_i + \TaskBlockingTime_i + \TaskInterferenceTime_i \le \TaskRelativeDeadline_i$$ {#eq-nervous-response-budget}
where $\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i$ is the worst-case execution time (WCET) of task $\RealTimeTaskIndex$, $\TaskBlockingTime_i$ is the maximum blocking time spent waiting for lower-priority tasks to vacate shared critical sections, $\TaskInterferenceTime_i$ is the maximum interference from preempting higher-priority tasks, timer interrupts, and DMA transfers, and $\TaskRelativeDeadline_i$ is the relative deadline.

Each term demands distinct evidentiary backing. Formal static timing analysis against an accurate cycle-level processor model can establish a bound on the WCET $\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i$. High-watermark profiling under stress-bench conditions instead characterizes observed execution times; it can refute a declared WCET but cannot establish one. The blocking term $\TaskBlockingTime_i$ represents the longest critical section of any lower-priority task that can lock a shared resource required by task $\RealTimeTaskIndex$. The priority ceiling protocol establishes a provable bound on $\TaskBlockingTime_i$. In this protocol, each synchronization lock carries a priority ceiling equal to the highest priority of any task that may acquire it. A task may acquire a lock only if its priority strictly exceeds the priority ceilings of all locks currently held by other tasks. Furthermore, any lock holder that blocks a higher-priority task temporarily inherits that task's elevated priority. Under these constraints, a task is blocked by at most a single lower-priority critical section across its entire execution [@sha1990priority]. An immediate priority ceiling protocol (IPCP), which instantly elevates a lock holder to the resource ceiling upon acquisition, guarantees the same blocking bound with lower runtime overhead. Finally, the interference term $\TaskInterferenceTime_i$ aggregates the execution time of all higher-priority tasks and interrupt service routines released during the response window. Because a longer response time provides a wider window for higher-priority tasks to re-trigger, calculating $\TaskInterferenceTime_i$ requires solving a fixed-point recurrence relation; @sec-appendix-systems-timers details this formulation, and @eq-nervous-response-budget defines the overarching budget that the recurrence resolves, which notebook \ref{nbk-nervous-response-margin} evaluates for the permission tick.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-rta-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RESPONSE-TIME BUDGET FOR THE PERMISSION TICK (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-rta-variance, the RTA example paragraph.
# │ Goal:    Compose R = C + B + I for the tick and compare with its deadline,
# │          then price a missed deadline in base travel.
# │ Show:    250 + 50 + 40 = 340 us <= 400 us deadline, 60 us margin; one
# │          missed period costs 1 ms, or 1.5 mm at the drive limit.
# │ How:     C, D, T from TickVocabulary (AISLE); B and I are scenario bounds.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_display_math, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class TickResponseBudget:
    """R = C + B + I for the permission tick against its deadline."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_wcet = TickVocabulary.t_wcet  # category: chosen (declared WCET)
    t_deadline = TickVocabulary.t_deadline  # category: chosen
    t_period = TickVocabulary.t_period  # category: chosen
    t_block = (
        AISLE.enforcer_blocking
    )  # category: illustrative (longest tick-masking section in lower-priority driver code; the seqlock adds none; scenario bound)
    t_interf = AISLE.enforcer_interference  # category: illustrative (timer and bus-interrupt work per response window; scenario bound)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_resp = (t_wcet + t_block + t_interf).to(microsecond)
    t_margin = (t_deadline - t_resp).to(microsecond)
    d_miss = (v * t_period).to(millimeter)  # travel during one extra period of detection delay

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_resp.magnitude - 340.0) < 1e-9, f"Tick response bound drifted: {t_resp}")
    check(abs(t_margin.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Tick response margin drifted: {t_margin}")
    check(t_resp <= t_deadline, "The tick's response bound must meet its deadline")
    check(abs(d_miss.magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Travel per missed period drifted: {d_miss}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_wcet_str = fmt_latency(t_wcet.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_block_str = fmt_latency(t_block, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_interf_str = fmt_latency(t_interf, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_resp_str = fmt_latency(t_resp, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_deadline_str = fmt_latency(t_deadline.to(microsecond), unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_miss_str = fmt_length(d_miss, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _us = lambda q: fmt(q, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    resp_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"R_i = C_i + B_i + I_i = {_us(t_wcet)} + {_us(t_block)} + {_us(t_interf)} = {_us(t_resp)}\ \mu\text{{s}} \le D_i = {_us(t_deadline)}\ \mu\text{{s}}, \quad D_i - R_i = {_us(t_margin)}\ \mu\text{{s}}"
    )
```

::: {#nbk-nervous-response-margin .callout-notebook title="The response-time margin"}

**Problem**: The permission tick must finish within its deadline after every release. With its declared WCET and illustrative bounds on blocking and interference, does it meet the deadline, and what happens to the margin when one term loses its bound?

**Variables**:

* Declared WCET $\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i =$ `{python} TickResponseBudget.t_wcet_str` and deadline $\TaskRelativeDeadline_i =$ `{python} TickResponseBudget.t_deadline_str` (both chosen).
* Blocking $\TaskBlockingTime_i =$ `{python} TickResponseBudget.t_block_str`, the longest section in which lower-priority code masks the tick, such as the link driver re-arming its DMA descriptor (illustrative). The mailbox adds nothing to $\TaskBlockingTime_i$, because the seqlock never makes the tick wait for the receive interrupt.
* Interference $\TaskInterferenceTime_i =$ `{python} TickResponseBudget.t_interf_str`, the timer and bus interrupts that can preempt the tick within one response window (illustrative).

**Math**:
`{python} TickResponseBudget.resp_math`

**Systems insight**: The margin is only as dependable as its weakest constituent bound. For instance, moving the mailbox copy into a low-priority task guarded by a standard mutex without priority inheritance or priority ceilings leaves $\TaskBlockingTime_i$ completely unbounded, because medium-priority work can preempt the lock holder indefinitely, which is the Mars Pathfinder pathology of war story \ref{ws-nervous-1997-mars-pathfinder-priority-inversion}. Similarly, permitting unscheduled DMA traffic on the tick's memory path destroys the upper bound on $\TaskInterferenceTime_i$. If even a single term loses its bound, the tick lacks a defensible worst-case response time, leaving the stopping budget's $\PermissionLoopPeriod$ parameter with no engineering foundation.

:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How host memory traffic would inflate the permission tick's interference if both paths shared one die is developed in @sec-placement-resource-contention.
:::

Neither a low average latency nor a modest processor utilization can substitute for that analytical bound,[^fn-math-liu-layland] because a single missed deadline degrades the machine across multiple architectural layers. When a deadline slips, distributed motor drives must hold their previous position setpoint for an entire additional bus cycle. Consequently, the actuator setpoint lags by a full period (`{python} TickResponseBudget.t_period_str`) rather than the conventional half-period delay associated with a zero-order hold. Repeated deadline misses manifest as timing jitter, which @cervin2003control analyze as a direct erosion of phase margin in digital feedback loops closed through the tick. Within the safety subsystem, a delayed tick evaluates an expired lease or safety violation late; at the drive velocity limit, each `{python} TickResponseBudget.t_period_str` delay incurs an irreversible loss of `{python} TickResponseBudget.d_miss_str` in physical stopping clearance.

[^fn-math-liu-layland]: **Rate-Monotonic Scheduling**\index{Rate-monotonic scheduling}: @liu1973scheduling established that static-priority rate-monotonic scheduling guarantees periodic task schedulability when total processor utilization satisfies $\TaskSetUtilization \le \PeriodicTaskCount(2^{1/\PeriodicTaskCount} - 1)$, converging to $\ln(2) \approx 0.693$ for large $\PeriodicTaskCount$. The utilization bound is sufficient, not necessary, so a task set that exceeds it may still meet every deadline; with shared-resource blocking and deadlines shorter than periods, only the exact response-time test of @sec-appendix-systems-timers decides.

Bounding these response terms requires categorizing every potential source of timing variability according to whether an analytical bound exists:

1. **Bounded Sources:** Hardware mechanisms that admit analytical upper bounds from vendor architectural specifications. Examples include deterministic instruction pipelines, round-robin interconnect arbitration, zero-wait-state tightly coupled memory (TCM/SRAM), and deterministic vectored interrupt controllers on real-time microcontrollers.
2. **Experimentally Characterized Sources:** Microarchitectural behaviors that cannot be proved strictly from first principles but can be enveloped empirically under frozen hardware configurations. Examples include bounded cache-line misses under hardware cache partitioning, write-buffer draining latencies, periodic DRAM auto-refresh pauses, and thermal throttling profiles stabilized by closed-loop active cooling.
3. **Unbounded Sources:** Software and hardware mechanisms that have no finite mathematical worst-case bound and must be purged from the real-time critical path. Examples include operating-system page faults under demand paging, preemptive thread synchronization lacking priority inheritance, dynamic heap allocation over fragmented memory pools, and unscheduled peripheral bus contention.

A credible timing guarantee must therefore explicitly enumerate all permissible operations along the execution path. While the hardware partitioning and core isolation strategies from @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning eliminate broad classes of timing interference, and a **zero-allocation static architecture**\index{Zero-allocation static architecture} pre-allocates all buffers and queues at boot time to eliminate memory-management overhead, these strategies cannot eliminate contention for shared memory buses. Response-time analysis must account for every remaining shared-resource transaction, because a high task priority alone never guarantees real-time execution, as the Mars Pathfinder resets showed.

::: {#ws-nervous-1997-mars-pathfinder-priority-inversion .callout-war-story title="The Mars Pathfinder priority inversion (1997)"}
**Context**: In July 1997, shortly after landing on Mars, the Mars Pathfinder spacecraft's avionics computer ran the VxWorks real-time operating system with preemptive priority-based scheduling across mission tasks [@reeves1997pathfinder].

**Mechanism**: A high-priority thread (`bc_dist`) distributed critical spacecraft bus telemetry, while a low-priority thread (`ASI/MET`) published meteorological sensor observations through a shared pipe. The mutex serializing access to this pipe was not explicitly declared in mission application code; rather, it was embedded deep within the operating system's `select()` implementation to protect internal file-descriptor queues [@reeves1997pathfinder]. When `ASI/MET` acquired this internal mutex, long-running medium-priority communications tasks preempted it. Because these medium-priority tasks outranked the meteorological thread, they starved it of CPU cycles, preventing it from releasing the mutex while `bc_dist` remained blocked, an unbounded priority inversion.

**Impact**: The blocked `bc_dist` thread missed its execution deadline. When the supervisory `bc_sched` watchdog initiated the subsequent bus cycle and detected that `bc_dist` had not completed, it flagged a critical timing fault and commanded a total system reset. Although telemetry collected prior to the reset survived in non-volatile storage, the resets recurred repeatedly during operational surface maneuvers.

**Response**: NASA engineers diagnosed the pathology on an identical ground testbed using VxWorks execution tracing, subsequently uploading an inflight software patch that enabled priority inheritance [@sha1990priority] on the underlying mutex semaphore.

**Systems lesson**: Preempting a low-priority lock holder with medium-priority work blocks high-priority consumers indefinitely. Priority inheritance resolves this vulnerability by temporarily elevating the lock holder's priority to match that of the blocked high-priority task, allowing it to complete its critical section promptly. In robotic actuator and motor-control paths, engineers must either rigorously bound blocking duration ($\TaskBlockingTime_i$) using priority inheritance protocols or eliminate shared locks altogether through lock-free communication structures.
:::

### Event-triggered and time-triggered bus architectures {#sec-nervous-fieldbus-architectures}

Once the permission tick finishes its check on the microcontroller, the admitted setpoint still has to cross a shared physical wire to reach the motor drives, where the same blocking and interference questions reappear. If a high-priority servo command arrives at a shared bus just after a lower-priority diagnostic frame has started transmitting, the command cannot preempt the bits already on the wire and must wait for the frame to finish. Physical buses handle shared medium access in one of two ways: on an event-triggered bus, nodes transmit whenever new data is ready and resolve collisions through dynamic bus arbitration, whereas on a time-triggered bus, a fixed global schedule assigns dedicated transmission windows to each node in advance. Neither design guarantees bounded delivery by its name alone; establishing a worst-case bound requires pricing payload sizes, competing traffic, error-recovery overhead, and device controller delays.

The Controller Area Network (CAN) and its CAN FD variant resolve message collisions via bitwise priority arbitration. While a high-priority frame preempts lower-priority traffic competing for an idle bus, it must wait for any frame already in transmission to finish. Switching to CAN FD accelerates payload serialization by elevating the data-phase bitrate, yet it retains the rule that an in-progress frame cannot be preempted. The blocking duration depends on the longest eligible frame at its nominal and data-phase rates. A valid worst-case response budget must therefore combine both the frame's own transmission time and the maximum duration of a lower-priority transmission already in progress.

EtherCAT adopts an on-the-fly time-triggered model: an Ethernet coordinator issues a single master frame that traverses all connected motor drives in a physical ring. Dedicated hardware controllers in each drive read incoming setpoints and write sensor feedback directly into designated bit offsets as the Ethernet frame streams through the physical layer. This architecture eliminates arbitration contention across the motor drives, while distributed clock synchronization synchronizes local PWM switching cycles. Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) achieves comparable determinism over switched Ethernet through IEEE 802.1Qbv time-aware traffic shapers. A TSN delivery guarantee relies on synchronized network gates, bounded clock skew, and strict admission controls that gate best-effort traffic.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The protocol engines and analytical response-time models of concrete fieldbus deployments are developed in @sec-appendix-systems-fieldbus.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_fieldbus_cycle_budget_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Schematic of two bus lines for three drives.
