A fieldbus path qualified under declared traffic and fault conditions bounds command delivery within its allocated cycle, but on-time delivery says nothing about whether the command should have been sent. That depends on which node may issue setpoints at all, and on whether each setpoint is checked against the machine's physical limits before it leaves.

## Actuation Authority {#sec-nervous-actuation-authority}

A shared mailbox cannot protect a mobile manipulator if the host processor retains a diagnostic route, an auxiliary bus master, or a JTAG debug port that writes directly to a drive. The silicon partition established in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning therefore requires exclusive physical control over every electrical path capable of energizing the motor windings. Actuation authority is this exclusive physical ability to modify drive states, encompassing PWM configuration registers, current references, gate-driver outputs, and bridge-enable lines. Under this architecture, the host publishes candidate proposals $\CandidateProposal_t$ and the safety microcontroller's permission path alone turns them into admitted commands $\AdmittedCommand_t$. The difference between holding that authority and merely appearing to is a question of wiring (@fig-04-privilege-enforcer-registers). When the permission path is the sole writer of the drive registers and can trip a drive inhibit, every motion passes its checks; when the host can also write those registers, one unchecked write reaches the motors and proposer and drives share a single failure domain.

::: {#fig-04-privilege-enforcer-registers fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Hardware proposal boundary**: (a) The application processor proposes across a black-channel board link into the safety microcontroller's own double buffer; the permission path on that microcontroller is the sole writer of the drive registers and can trip a drive inhibit. (b) When the application processor can write the drive registers directly, an unchecked write reaches the motors, and proposer and drives share a single failure domain." fig-alt="Two panels. (a) Separate permission path: a dashed bronze application processor box, learned proposers with no drive access, sends proposal p t through a dashed black-channel board link with CRC and sequence into a safety MCU container, which has its own memory and is the sole writer of drive registers. Inside it, an MCU-local double buffer feeds the permission path at a 1 kHz tick, which checks state, freshness, and lease. The permission path sends admitted command u t to drive registers and then drives and motors; a red trip line from the permission path sends drive inhibit to the drives and motors. (b) Collapsed, host writes drives: inside a red dashed box labeled one failure domain, the application processor sends an unchecked register write straight to the drive registers, which feed the drives and motors."}
![](images/svg/fig04_privilege_enforcer_registers.svg){width="90%"}
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How exclusive authority over each actuator channel passes between the learned policy, an operator, and the fallback is developed in @sec-intervention-discrete-states.
:::

The microcontroller continuously evaluates physical safety invariants: verifying that commanded joint positions lie within certified reach envelopes, that joint velocities stay within qualified limits, and that projected decelerations remain safely within dynamic stopping clearance ($\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$). When a proposal satisfies all invariants, the microcontroller admits the command and interpolates waypoints into cyclic position setpoints for each bus cycle, which the drives track through their internal velocity and current loops. When a candidate proposal violates an invariant or expires, the enforcer refuses it ($\bot$). A refusal does not automatically revoke a previously admitted, actively executing trajectory chunk. Instead, the active chunk continues running as long as its state, sensor evidence, and chunk lease remain valid. When those conditions lapse or fail, the enforcer terminates execution authority and transitions the system into a controlled deceleration or hold. In parallel, a separate hardware trip zone stands ready to cut motor drive torque upon catastrophic electrical faults, though simply de-energizing an inverter does not by itself brake moving mass.[^fn-hw-tripzone-break]

[^fn-hw-tripzone-break]: **Hardware Trip Zone**\index{Hardware trip zone}: Microcontroller hardware trip zones couple analog overcurrent and overvoltage comparators directly to timer output logic. Upon fault detection, configured trip logic may force gate signals high-impedance or activate a validated braking mode. These have different mechanical consequences: torque removal can leave the plant coasting, while dynamic braking requires a rated energy path.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The refusal authority and the state invariants it checks are developed in @sec-enforcement-authority-refuse.
:::

At the causal boundary the root cause of an aberrant proposal does not matter. A remote memory exploit in a host operating system daemon, an adversarial optical perturbation that induces a vision model hallucination, and an arithmetic overflow in an acceleration tensor engine can all produce invalid proposals for the same boundary filter to reject. A proposal that passes the physical checks may still pursue the wrong task, so admission does not establish semantic correctness. Because the enforcer evaluates physical invariant bounds against direct sensor feedback from optical encoders and current shunts rather than inspecting internal neural network weights, it requires no internal model of why the proposer failed. Because the host lacks bus-master privileges to actuator registers, a compromised host has no bypass around this check. Complete protection against a rogue host nonetheless requires four physical foundations: independent sensing, an accurate kinematic and dynamic limit model, sufficient actuator capability, and a physically feasible fallback trajectory.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The causal boundary, where a command becomes current in a winding and mass begins to move, is established in @sec-boundary-tensors-to-silicon.
:::

Controlled stopping and torque removal impose fundamentally different engineering obligations. Powered braking actively uses the drive inverters to decelerate the plant to zero velocity before disabling torque. Immediate torque removal, by contrast, de-energizes the motor windings instantly, which can leave a wheeled base coasting uncontrollably or allow a vertically loaded manipulator arm to collapse under gravity. Maintaining a held position requires either continuous motor torque or a certified mechanical restraint. At the actuation authority interface, the systems designer must explicitly designate the physical fallback response and reserve both the execution time and thermal energy budget that it demands.

A refusal that leaves no admissible active continuation carries an unavoidable physical cost. When the enforcer rejects an invalid proposal and commands dynamic braking on a fast-moving joint, the physical braking path must supply sufficient torque, clearance, and thermal dissipation capacity to arrest the moving mass. Over an arrest interval spanning several hundred milliseconds, the motor winding resistance, dynamic brake chopper resistor, or friction brake lining must absorb the joint's accumulated kinetic energy within the thermal limits detailed in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles. This dissipation must occur without degrading winding insulation or permitting the manipulator to breach its physical clearance boundary.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The stopping-distance model this braking path must satisfy is developed in @sec-appendix-systems-stopping.
:::

If the safety microcontroller itself hangs or suffers a clock failure, it cannot execute a software-directed stop. A hardwired, out-of-band interlock must therefore supervise the system and enforce a qualified fallback state. Safe Torque Off (STO) accomplishes this by disabling gate-driver optocouplers or charge pumps through hardware logic, preventing the inverter from generating rotating magnetic fields.[^fn-std-iec61800-sto] STO does not isolate the high-voltage DC bus from the mains, nor does it guarantee that momentum will dissipate within the stopping clearance allocated for powered deceleration. Complete electrical isolation requires an upstream safety contactor, and containing gravitational drop or mechanical drift requires a certified electromechanical brake. A dual-channel interlock circuit, the relay network @fig-real-estop diagrams, decouples torque inhibition entirely from the host software stack; safety qualification must still verify that the system remains resilient against common-cause failures in power rails, clock crystals, and harness wiring.

[^fn-std-iec61800-sto]: **Safe Torque Off (STO)**\index{Safe torque off}: An STO implementation removes torque-producing drive signals through a hardware interlock. An IEC 61800-5-2 integrity rating depends on the actual devices, diagnostic coverage, wiring, and validation, not on the circuit pattern alone [@iec61800part52].

::: {#fig-real-estop fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative out-of-band interlock and STO path**: Each emergency-stop contact holds its own force-guided relay, and each relay's enable contact holds one of the drive's two STO inputs, so a single welded contact or shorted wire leaves the other channel able to remove torque. The EDM contacts report a relay that failed to release before restart. Removing torque leaves the motor free to coast; the spring-applied brake is a separate circuit that clamps when its supply is removed. The diagram shows a hardware response path, not a certified integrity level or a stopping distance (synthesized from ISO 13849-1 and IEC 61800-5-2)." fig-alt="Two-channel schematic. A red positive-break E-stop is mechanically linked to two normally closed contacts, S1 and S2, each fed from 24 volts. S1 feeds the coil of force-guided relay K1 and S2 the coil of relay K2; each relay has a normally open enable contact and a normally closed EDM contact. K1 sends STO1 enable and K2 sends STO2 enable to two STO terminals on the drive, which feed the gate-drive supply and then the inverter bridge driving motor M. A red tag above the motor reads tau equals 0, and a note below reads may coast. The two EDM contacts are wired in series with a dashed teal line to a reset monitor, restart only if K1 and K2 released. At the bottom, a brake supply on its own circuit, switched by K1 and K2, contacts not drawn, feeds a spring brake that clamps on power loss and acts on the motor shaft. A note reads hardware only, no processor in this path."}
![](images/svg/fig04_sto_safety_circuit.svg){width="100%"}
:::

In @fig-real-estop, dual positive-break E-stop contacts ($\EmergencyStopContact_1$, $\EmergencyStopContact_2$) drive independent force-guided relays ($\ForceGuidedRelay_1$, $\ForceGuidedRelay_2$), routing dual STO enable signals into the motor drive while series-wired normally closed external device monitoring (EDM) contacts prevent system restart if either relay fails to open. At the bottom, a dedicated brake supply drops a spring-applied mechanical brake directly onto the motor shaft upon power loss, enforcing torque removal ($\MotorTorque = 0$) and holding restraint without software or processor intervention. However, engineers must not confuse a static holding brake with a dynamic stopping brake. Under normal operational sequences, the drive decelerates the motor to zero velocity electrically before engaging the spring brake to hold position. Dropping a holding brake onto a spinning shaft during a high-speed emergency stop subjects the brake pads and hub to severe friction heating and mechanical shock, requiring independent thermal rating and stopping-distance validation. The stop-category selections and timing sequences depend directly on these electromechanical limits.

::: {#psp-nervous-hardware-authority .callout-perspective title="Hardware authority invariant"}
If an unverified learned policy has direct memory-mapped write access to actuator gate-driver registers, the machine has no mediated proposal path, and its next out-of-distribution input reaches the motors unchecked.
:::

Write privilege is a physical reality dictated by memory mapping, bus arbitration, and physical trace layout, never a configurable software flag. The host processor holds no write privilege to drive registers. While hardware partitioning determines which processor may issue physical commands to an actuator, the engineer must still decide what physical quantity those admitted commands specify, because each choice leaves a different set of failure modes for the permission path to catch.

### What a proposal may command {#sec-nervous-command-interface}

A digital motor drive accepts setpoints across a nested cascade of control loops: position, velocity, and winding current, with current running innermost at the highest bandwidth. Sending raw current targets directly to the drive bypasses its position and velocity loops and leaves the permission path to predict how gravity, inertia, and external contact will move the joint, whereas sending pure position targets lets the drive bound its own speed and current at the cost of ramping winding current against an unmodeled obstacle until the inverter saturates or the mechanism breaks. The level at which a proposal enters this cascade therefore decides which physical states the drive hardware regulates on its own and which quantities the permission path must verify before admitting the command. Four command interfaces dominate physical AI systems, each placing a different prediction and checking burden on the enforcer.

A *position target* $\JointPositionTarget$ delegates the entire trajectory tracking problem to the drive's internal cascaded loops. Because the drive firmware enforces its own configured speed and current limits, the enforcer's verification burden remains relatively compact: it validates that the target lies within the geometric reach envelope, bounds the discrete step between consecutive targets (which position gains convert directly into velocity and torque demands), and ensures adequate dynamic stopping clearance. However, a pure position target cannot modulate interaction force. When encountering an unmodeled rigid obstacle, a stiff proportional-integral position loop interprets physical contact as a tracking error to be eliminated, ramping winding current until the inverter saturates or the mechanical structure breaks; the impedance-control analysis in @sec-body-transmission-compliance quantified this exact failure mode on a cage-door latch.

A *velocity target* $\JointVelocityTarget$ shifts kinematic integration to the host proposer, bypassing the drive's position loop. Because the proposal omits an explicit geometric endpoint, the enforcer cannot simply validate a target coordinate against static workspace limits. Instead, the enforcer forward-integrates the commanded velocity over the duration of the active chunk lease to predict the joint's worst-case state at lease expiration. It then checks both the reach envelope and the dynamic stopping distance against this forward projection. As with pure position control, contact force remains unregulated, and unmodeled collisions will produce maximum drive torque.

A *torque target* $\JointTorqueTarget$, delivered as a direct current reference, bypasses both outer loops. The drive regulates only electromagnetic winding current. Consequently, all kinematic state evolution, including velocity, position, and braking distance, becomes an emergent consequence of plant dynamics, gravity, and external contact forces rather than an enforced setpoint. The enforcer must bound the resulting state evolution and preserve a feasible fallback, using a plant model or effort-space constraints, while constraining torque slew rates and tracking the cumulative mechanical energy injected into the system. Torque control offers maximum responsiveness for dynamic locomotion and manipulation, but it imposes the heaviest computational burden on the permission path while providing the least explicit intent.

An *impedance target* specifies a virtual equilibrium pose alongside stiffness gains $\PidProportionalGain$ and damping gains $\PidDerivativeGain$, so the actuator behaves as a virtual spring-damper [@hogan1985impedance], the same model introduced in @sec-body-transmission-compliance:
$$\ImpedanceRestoringForce = \PidProportionalGain (\ImpedanceEquilibriumPosition - \ImpedanceControlledPosition) + \PidDerivativeGain (\ImpedanceEquilibriumVelocity - \ImpedanceControlledVelocity)$$
Its dynamic dual, an *admittance target*, measures external contact force via load cells and commands motion in response. Both formulations explicitly regulate the dynamic relationship between motion and force, a coupling that position, velocity, and torque interfaces leave unconstrained. This capability makes impedance and admittance formulations standard in contact-rich manipulation tasks. The enforcer's verification role expands accordingly: it must evaluate both the equilibrium setpoint and the commanded stiffness gains. Under quasi-static contact, the maximum contact force is bounded by the product of the commanded stiffness and the largest displacement the environment can impose. Consequently, a stiffness parameter that exceeds the structural limits of the workpiece or fixture is just as inadmissible as a trajectory crossing a workspace wall. However, steady-state gains do not govern transient impact forces, which depend heavily on approach velocity, rotor inertia, structural compliance, and control-loop latency. @Sec-enforcement-intentional-contact establishes the energy and contact-force barriers needed to bound these transient impact phases.

On the reference mobile manipulator, the enforcer admits position waypoints, interpolating them into fine setpoints for each bus cycle while the motor drives close their own internal velocity and current loops. When the manipulator engages the sprung latch of an equipment cage door, the host switches to an impedance command, introducing stiffness and damping parameters that the real-time tick must validate before transmission. No command interface eliminates the verification burden of the permission path: shifting the command interface inward, from position setpoints toward raw current references, strips away explicit geometric intent and forces the safety layer to predict complex electrodynamic behavior. Write privilege and command filtering protect the physical plant only if the enforcer also maintains physical independence from the host whose proposals it evaluates, because if the safety microcontroller and the host application processor share a power rail, a common system clock, or a unified memory bus, a failure in the host can brown out the microcontroller, corrupt its timing, or deadlock the bus, silencing the safety layer without issuing a single illegal drive command.

## Hardware Isolation and Fault Containment {#sec-nervous-hardware-isolation}

A large current transient during a neural accelerator burst can pull down a shared power rail and brown out or reset the permission processor without warning, while memory bus contention on a shared interconnect can delay safety checks past the hard real-time execution tick. Even when safety enforcement executes on a dedicated processor, physical coupling to the proposal engine can silently undermine software isolation. Containing faults across the two paths therefore requires isolating or bounding shared physical resources across four domains: execution hardware, reference oscillators, power distribution rails, and memory hierarchies.[^fn-std-iso26262-ffi] Where any of those resources remain shared, the architecture must demonstrate that cross-domain interference and declared common-cause faults cannot prevent the permission path from meeting its execution deadline or initiating its qualified fallback.

[^fn-std-iso26262-ffi]: **Freedom from Interference (FFI)**\index{Freedom from interference}: ISO 26262 defines FFI in its vocabulary, Part 1, as the absence of cascading failures between two or more elements that could lead to the violation of a safety requirement [@iso26262]. Part 6 lists the software interference it covers (timing and execution, memory, and exchange of information), whereas shared power, clocks, and heat are common-cause and cascading faults that Part 9 treats in its dependent-failure analysis and that IEC 61508 addresses as independence between elements [@iec61508-2-2010]. A neural policy sharing silicon with the permission path therefore needs both arguments, FFI for its software and a dependent-failure analysis for the resources underneath.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-permission-rail
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SHARED DRIVE BUS VS. THE HELD-UP PERMISSION RAIL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation, the design-choice paragraph
# │          (the full four-coupling inventory lives in @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die).
# │ Goal:    Name the bus the application processor shares with the drives and
# │          the isolated, held-up rail the permission path runs on instead.
# │ Show:    47.7 V nominal drive bus, 42 V depleted, the application
# │          processor's converter locking out at 33 V, 2 s hold-up.
# │ How:     Registry fields on RM (M6: 48 V drive bus, MiR250-class pack,
# │          MEAN WELL DDR-240C-24 converter). The sustained sag screen is
# │          derived in @sec-body-power-integrity, and the hold-up is sized in
# │          @sec-body-permission-rail-isolation.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_voltage, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PermissionRail:
    """The permission path's isolated, held-up rail beside the shared drive bus."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_bus_nom = RM.drive_bus_nominal  # category: datasheet (48 V-class pack, nominal)
    v_bus_low = RM.drive_bus_battery_low  # category: datasheet (pack minimum)
    v_uvlo = RM.drive_bus_uvlo  # category: datasheet (converter input lockout)
    t_holdup = RM.permission_rail_holdup  # category: chosen (permission-rail hold-up)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_headroom_low = (v_bus_low - v_uvlo).to(volt)  # headroom a depleted pack starts with

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_bus_nom.to(volt).magnitude - 47.7) < 1e-9, f"Drive bus nominal drifted: {v_bus_nom}")
    check(abs(v_uvlo.to(volt).magnitude - 33.0) < 1e-9, f"Converter lockout drifted: {v_uvlo}")
    check(abs(t_holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Permission-rail hold-up drifted: {t_holdup}")
    check(abs(v_headroom_low.magnitude - 9.0) < 1e-9, "Even a depleted pack starts 9 V above the converter lockout")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_bus_nom_str = fmt_voltage(v_bus_nom, unit=volt, precision=1)
    v_uvlo_str = fmt_voltage(v_uvlo, unit=volt, precision=0)
    t_holdup_str = fmt_latency(t_holdup, unit=second, precision=0)
```

The running machine's two-processor architecture addresses each of these four fault paths with an explicit hardware design choice. The permission path executes from private memory over a dedicated board-level link, clocks from an independent oscillator, and draws power from the isolated rail specified in @sec-body-permission-rail-isolation rather than from the primary `{python} PermissionRail.v_bus_nom_str` drive bus feeding the application processor. Diode-isolated storage capacitors hold up this safety rail for `{python} PermissionRail.t_holdup_str`. If a transient load fault pulls the drive bus down to the host converter's undervoltage lockout threshold at `{python} PermissionRail.v_uvlo_str`, the safety microcontroller stays powered long enough to capture the undervoltage interrupt, log the event, and command a graceful fallback while the primary host resets, provided that the required detector, actuator power, and braking path survive the fault.

Keeping the logic powered does not guarantee motor torque or braking capability. Bringing a moving machine to a controlled stop requires sufficient DC bus energy, healthy inverter stages, and adequate obstacle clearance. If electrical drive power collapses entirely, the system must execute a qualified unpowered fallback whose mechanical brake engagement delay and subsequent stopping motion fit within the pre-allocated physical envelope. These isolation guarantees are design assertions that must be empirically verified on physical hardware. Every shared dependency must be carried forward into the formal verification handoff record.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The four substrate couplings that board layout must sever, and the fault-injection experiments that test their isolation, are developed in @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_substrate_blast_radius.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Blast-radius sketch: a red square labeled drive bus sag sends arrows to two red dots labeled motor drives and host lockout 33 V. A dashed branch toward a green dot labeled permission rail, 2 s hold-up, ends at a green bar before reaching it."}

*A sag on the shared bus reaches every load; the permission rail rides through on its own.*
:::

Substrate isolation ensures that the permission path stays alive when the host crashes, but the enforcer's downstream action depends entirely on how the proposer failed: through unresponsiveness or through corruption. Unresponsiveness occurs when an inference pipeline deadlocks, thread scheduling misses a deadline, or kernel memory fragmentation stalls process execution, yielding no new trajectory packets. A complete host crash trips the hardware heartbeat timer. Conversely, the host operating system might remain healthy while the user-space neural policy pipeline hangs; in that scenario, the proposer simply stops emitting admissible action chunks, allowing the active chunk's lease or evidence deadline to lapse. These complementary deadlines form the supervisory timing hierarchy established in @sec-nervous-supervisory-timers.

Corruption occurs when the proposer continues running and satisfies its heartbeat deadline, but outputs invalid or hazardous setpoints. Examples include kinematically unreachable joint configurations, step discontinuities in velocity requests, or floating-point NaNs and infinities caused by out-of-distribution visual tokens or matrix overflow. The enforcer handles these two failure profiles through orthogonal mechanisms: unresponsiveness triggers trajectory revocation as soon as the chunk lease or the heartbeat timer expires, whereas corruption prompts an immediate invariant rejection at the boundary filter upon the arrival of the malformed packet. A live heartbeat therefore never extends motion authority; only an admitted chunk renews it, and authority ends when the chunk lease runs out. Whether the chunk policy can renew quickly enough to keep the machine moving, and why the slower intent model supplies goals rather than holding chunk leases itself, is the coupled budget of @sec-nervous-coupled-budget.

When active motion authority lapses without an admissible continuation, the permission path must execute an explicit degradation strategy rather than cutting motor bus power unconditionally. As detailed in @sec-body-unpowered-states, de-energizing an inverter drops the actuators into uncontrolled freewheeling or dynamic short-circuit braking, neither of which produces an orderly, predictable stop. Instead, the safety path evaluates the plant's instantaneous kinematic state and selects the safest feasible deceleration profile. An optional brief continuation along the last validated trajectory is permissible only while its state estimates, sensor evidence validity, chunk lease window, and obstacle clearance margins all remain valid.

Once that lease expires, any separately authorized fallback delay $\FallbackHold$ is absorbed into the total reaction latency $\PrebrakeDelay$ and must fit, together with the evidence age, within the `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling_left_str` left under the pre-brake ceiling once the lease path and brake onset are charged at the drive limit (notebook \ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}). If measured latency bounds exceed this headroom, the enforcer must initiate deceleration sooner. Controlled braking uses the available actuator torque characterized in @sec-body-actuator-limits to arrest motion within the remaining clearance. On gravity-loaded manipulators, motion arrest must be backed by engaging rated mechanical holding brakes once the joints reach standstill, preventing gravitational backdriving when drive power is subsequently removed.

After the physical plant comes to a complete halt, the architecture executes a **recovery handshake**\index{Recovery handshake} before restoring autonomous proposal authority. The safety microcontroller asserts a persistent `FAULT_HELD` latch in its exported status register and publishes the plant's confirmed physical rest pose $(\RestConfiguration, \GeneralizedVelocities = \ZeroVector)$. In turn, the application processor must discard all pending action chunks, invalidate internal state tied to the interrupted motion, capture fresh sensor observations tagged with synchronized hardware timestamps, and formulate a newly aligned trajectory proposal.

This recovery sequence must also purge any proposal-side state that assumes the robot executed its planned trajectory to completion. For autoregressive policies and VLA models, this requires flushing token buffers and the key-value (KV) attention cache; retaining pre-fault keys and values would bias future action generation toward a physical trajectory that was interrupted. However, clearing software caches does not by itself establish physical continuity. Before deasserting the `FAULT_HELD` latch and restoring proposal authority, the safety microcontroller inspects the opening waypoint $\ProposalFirstWaypoint$ of the incoming proposal, verifying that it aligns with the robot's measured physical rest pose within a strict spatial bound ($||\ProposalFirstWaypoint - \RestConfiguration|| \le \RecoveryPoseTolerance$).

Architectural independence cannot simply be read off a schematic or block diagram; it must be empirically validated against identified common-cause faults on the physical board. Similarly, the chunk lease that constrains a malfunctioning proposer derives directly from physical dynamics, sized from the stopping margin that remains after detection delays and actuator responses. Together, these defenses bound a proposer that crashes, stalls, or publishes corrupted actions. The separation leaves one question open, whether a neural policy engineered to execute deterministically at the enforcer's own update rate still requires an external runtime monitor.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The fault injection that tests this independence on the physical board is developed in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

## Invariant Checking {#sec-nervous-invariant-checking}

A proposer fast enough to keep pace with the permission tick invites a shortcut. Learned locomotion controllers already emit joint targets within an order of magnitude of a millisecond, and a designer may be tempted to let such a policy write the motor registers directly. Rate does not confer authority. A fast network emitting joint targets or torques carries the same statistical uncertainty as a large model generating waypoints a few times a second, and even when policy and enforcer share one period, the network's output remains a proposal that must pass the proposal boundary before it changes current in a winding. What the permission path can still guarantee when a learned policy commands at control rate, and what it gives up, is examined in @sec-enforcement-thesis-bends.

The interface must reject an inadmissible candidate without waiting for the producer, and recheck the active command against current physical state. Position and velocity limits ($\GeneralizedCoordinates \in [\JointPositionLowerLimit, \JointPositionUpperLimit]$ and $|\GeneralizedVelocities| \le \JointVelocityLimit$) are necessary but do not by themselves establish a feasible stop. A torque-slew constraint, $|\JointTorqueSlew| = |(\JointTorque_k - \JointTorque_{k-1})/\FiniteChange \TimeInstant| \le \JointTorqueSlewLimit$, can limit command changes, but a command that meets the slew limit must still satisfy the other physical limits. Contact may additionally require accounting for exchanged energy, $\int \JointTorque^\top \GeneralizedVelocities\,d\TimeInstant$.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The passivity framework that accounts for energy exchanged in contact is developed in @sec-appendix-control-passivity.
:::

Choosing and composing those filters is the work of @sec-enforcement, which constructs the admissibility calculation and selects a feasible continuation, hold, or stop. What the Nervous System fixes is the execution contract those filters must run under, whatever they compute. On the running machine the contract has numbers. The recheck of the active command must finish inside the tick's `{python} TickVocabulary.t_deadline_str` deadline under the response bound of @eq-nervous-response-budget, it must read measured wheel and joint encoder state rather than commanded setpoints (the fallacy of @sec-nervous-fallacies-pitfalls shows what the commanded setpoints miss), and it must leave the safety microcontroller the only writer of the drive registers. Neither fast inference nor a fast rejection routine establishes that contract on its own.

The same reasoning covers the one proposer that is not learned. A remote operator is a third proposer. Its commands pass the same permission path, and network delay spends the same pre-brake budget. Neither speed nor a human origin gives a proposal authority; only passing the permission path's checks does, and each check spends part of a budget that the next section lays out handoff by handoff.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How an operator's reaction and link delays are charged against the stopping budget is developed in @sec-intervention-reaction-drift.
:::

::: {#chk-nervous-hardware-invariants .callout-checkpoint title="Hardware isolation and invariant checking"}

Before turning to the handoffs between proposer and actuator, verify your understanding of the exchange, hardware isolation, and pre-actuation invariant defenses:

- [ ] **Nonblocking exchange**: Can you explain how the seqlock reader detects a torn read in one bounded attempt, and why a writer stopped mid-write cannot extend the active spline's state, evidence, or lease validity?
- [ ] **Independence as a hypothesis**: Can you state the independence requirement the permission path must meet, and explain why the two-processor split satisfies it only once loaded tests on the machine's silicon support the claim?
- [ ] **Chunk lease cost**: Can you explain why the chunk lease must be sized from stopping distance and clearance rather than chosen as a software timeout, why a heartbeat never renews it, and how much clear distance lengthening it from `{python} CheckpointEstimates.t_lease_str` to `{python} CheckpointEstimates.t_lease_new_str` would spend at the `{python} CheckpointEstimates.v_str` drive limit?
- [ ] **Command interface**: Can you state what the permission path must check or predict for a position, a velocity, a torque, and an impedance target, and why a velocity target leaves it to predict motion over the whole lease?
- [ ] **Rate matching and authority**: Can you explain why a policy that runs at the plant's own rate still produces only proposals, and what timing, state, and fallback obligations remain?

:::

## The Handoffs Matrix {#sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix}

When a mobile manipulator overruns a stop, the diagnosis begins by locating the fault at one of five canonical handoffs between the photons collected by its cameras and the current delivered to its drives. A cloud service governs its interfaces with statistical service-level objectives (SLOs), such as a $\text{p99}$ request latency; when a tail event violates that target, the runtime absorbs the delay through retries, request rerouting, or graceful degradation. The five handoffs of an embodied machine define **hard cyber-physical service-level objectives** instead. Software cannot recall physical momentum or undo resistive heating in an actuator winding, so no retry mechanism can mask an unbudgeted interface violation.

Upstream, sensing hardware transfers raw transducer signals to perception pipelines. Perception yields intermediate geometric and semantic representations that fuse into an estimated world state. This state feeds the learned policy to produce an action plan, which in turn submits candidate trajectories to the safety enforcer. Finally, the approved command passes from the enforcer to the physical motor drives. Across each boundary, five interface limits govern feasibility: latency ($\Latency$), bandwidth ($\Bandwidth$), energy and heat ($\HeatDissipationPower$), determinism ($\TimingJitter$), and fault domain isolation ($\FaultDomainIsolation$). The five handoffs and five interface limits form a five-by-five matrix mapping every signal path to the physical budgets of the machine. These interface limits are distinct from the body's five mechanical budgets, which enter the matrix primarily through its latency and energy columns. The contract that records these budgets, the handoff record defined below, joins the physical limit records of @sec-body-limit-record-schema to the proposer limits of the Brain, so latency, renewal rate, and evidence age are written in one schema.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The body's five mechanical budgets are established in @sec-body-five-budgets.
:::

The allocation in @tbl-04-synthesis-grid illustrates which limits are design-limiting at each handoff, using chosen design budgets rather than empirical measurements. The matrix gathers the physical budgets of the machine's mechanical, cognitive, and sensory systems, together with the sensor capture that the five-level machine model places at the Boundary. In the Boundary row ($\SignalHandoff_1$), where the physical world becomes digital measurement, bandwidth and latency bind first: raw multi-camera pixel streams saturate the serializer-deserializer (SerDes) lanes, and the exposure window imposes a strict floor on image age before serialization even begins. The Brain rows ($\SignalHandoff_2$, $\SignalHandoff_3$) bind first on energy and latency, reflecting the heavy inference costs of the learned proposers. The Body row ($\SignalHandoff_5$) binds first on determinism and heat, because the drives' current loops must hold their timing jitter below $10\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$, and every ampere delivered dissipates heat across the windings and power inverter stages.

The Nervous System row ($\SignalHandoff_4$) forms the architectural bridge coupling the Brain and the Body. The proposal boundary between the learned planner and the enforcer carries an action proposal ($\CandidateProposal_t$), typically structured as a compact spline parameterization or waypoint chunk. For the compact payload assumed in this grid, the required throughput is modest ($\Bandwidth < 100\text{ kB/s}$), so bandwidth does not bind; instead, latency, determinism ($\TimingJitter$), and fault domain isolation ($\FaultDomainIsolation$) govern the interface. The permission path isolates stochastic model proposals using nonblocking mailboxes and expiring leases. On the mobile manipulator, the latency limit is the chunk lease, which consumes `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str` of the `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling_str` pre-brake ceiling available at the drive limit (@sec-nervous-lease-sizing), while the active command is rechecked within each `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_tick_str` permission tick. Full trajectory admission has a separate computation and response budget and must complete before any candidate chunk activates; the tick interval does not imply that arbitrary occupancy queries or whole-trajectory collision checks fit within that brief slice. Fault isolation relies on a private peripheral bus, an independent oscillator, and the isolated, held-up power rail detailed in @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation.

From the causal boundary perspective, any interface failure localizes to the specific handoff and budget it violates. Semantic mistakes or flawed physical assumptions can still escape an otherwise timely interface; the matrix does not substitute for task-level evaluation or hazard analysis. When diagnosing an over-budget stop, trajectory overrun, or subsystem fault, engineers navigate @tbl-04-synthesis-grid through a three-step operational root-cause procedure:

1. *Locate the boundary seam:* Identify which physical handoff ($\SignalHandoff_1\text{--}\SignalHandoff_5$) recorded the initial timing excursion, sequence gap, torn payload, or thermal trip.
2. *Check the binding dimension:* Query the specific physical limit ($\Latency, \Bandwidth, \HeatDissipationPower, \TimingJitter, \FaultDomainIsolation$) designated as *BINDING* for that handoff cell, identifying the primary resource bottleneck governing the interface.
3. *Evaluate like-for-like evidence:* Compare runtime diagnostic traces directly against the recorded bound kind (`requirement`, `proven bound`, or `measured distribution`), verifying whether the failure stemmed from an unmodeled microarchitectural tail event or a direct physical budget violation.

A handoff diagnosis must strictly compare like evidence. For the $\SignalHandoff_2$ state-estimation path, suppose engineers allocate a $30.0\text{ ms}$ latency budget and measure $\text{p99} = 24.5\text{ ms}$ during a baseline hardware-in-the-loop run, yielding a sampled margin of $+5.5\text{ ms}$. Under thermal throttling, a subsequent run measuring $\text{p99} = 85.0\text{ ms}$ reveals a $-55.0\text{ ms}$ deficit against that design budget. The appropriate remedy is to reduce or reallocate computational workload while preserving independent safety enforcement during revalidation. A sampled $\text{p99}$ latency diagnoses a performance regression; it does not constitute a worst-case timing proof.

| Canonical Handoff Boundary                                     | Latency Limit ($\Latency$)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Bandwidth Limit ($\Bandwidth$)                                                                                        | Energy & Heat Limit ($\HeatDissipationPower$)                                                                           | Determinism Limit ($\TimingJitter$)                                                                                  | Fault Domain Isolation ($\FaultDomainIsolation$)                                                |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **$\SignalHandoff_1$: Sensing $\to$ Perception** *(Boundary)*  | **BINDING** \newline $\Latency \le 16.7\text{ ms}$, one frame period (sensor age dated at the frame's middle row; the oldest row is older, @sec-perception-observation-contract)                                                                                                                                                                      | **BINDING** \newline $\Bandwidth \ge 1.2\text{ GB/s}$ (multi-camera 4K uncompressed streams)                          | *Non-binding* \newline $\HeatDissipationPower < 3\text{ W}$ (sensor head dissipation isolated)                          | **BINDING** \newline $\TimingJitter \le 1.0\text{ ms}$ (frame-sync triggers prevent skew)                            | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by SerDes hardware & DMA ring buffers                           |
| **$\SignalHandoff_2$: Perception $\to$ State** *(Brain)*       | **BINDING** \newline $\Latency \le 30.0\text{ ms}$ (camera and inertial motion estimate & feature window)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | *Non-binding* \newline $\Bandwidth\approx 10\text{--}50\text{ MB/s}$ (compressed image features & 3D occupancy cells) | **BINDING** \newline $\HeatDissipationPower \approx 15\text{--}35\text{ W}$ (edge vision backbone accelerator envelope) | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by sliding-window state estimator buffers                                            | **BINDING** \newline Spatial memory isolation: MPUs prevent memory corruption                   |
| **$\SignalHandoff_3$: State $\to$ Plan** *(Brain)*             | **BINDING** \newline chunk policy `{python} MachineStallTravel.t_chunk_str` p99 inside its `{python} MachineTiers.t_chunk_period_str` renewal period (@sec-brain-two-proposers); autoregressive intent model `{python} MachineStallTravel.t_intent_str` inside its `{python} MachineTiers.t_intent_period_str` period (@sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline) | *Non-binding* \newline $\Bandwidth < 5\text{ MB/s}$ (low-dimensional state & prompt embeddings)                       | **BINDING** \newline $\HeatDissipationPower \approx 30\text{--}75\text{ W}$ (transformer/diffusion matrix accelerators) | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by receding-horizon chunking & spline buffers                                        | **BINDING** \newline Host faults must not halt the independent permission path                  |
| **$\SignalHandoff_4$: Plan $\to$ Enforcer** *(Nervous System)* | **BINDING** \newline chunk lease `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str` (candidate allocation; age at admission from @tbl-04-event-timing); active-command checks within each `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_tick_str` tick; full admission budget recorded separately                                                                             | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by compact parameterized splines ($\Bandwidth < 100\text{ kB/s}$)                     | *Non-binding* \newline $\HeatDissipationPower < 0.5\text{ W}$ (fixed-point constraint evaluation on MCU)                | **BINDING** \newline $\TimingJitter \le 100\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ (cycle-deterministic packet reception on MCU) | **BINDING** \newline Hardware boundary: private bus, separate oscillator, isolated held-up rail |
| **$\SignalHandoff_5$: Enforcer $\to$ Actuator** *(Body)*       | **BINDING** \newline $\Latency \le$ `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_tick_str` (servo interval `{python} TickDelayBudget.t_bus_str`; current loop `{python} MachineTiers.t_current_str`)                                                                                                                                                                   | *Non-binding* \newline $\Bandwidth\approx 1\text{--}5\text{ Mbps}$ (cyclic packets over deterministic command bus)    | **BINDING** \newline $\WindingCurrent^2 \ElectricalResistance$ copper winding dissipation, MOSFET switching losses      | **BINDING** \newline $\TimingJitter < 10\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$ (hard real-time PWM phase alignment & FOC)       | **BINDING** \newline Galvanic isolation, out-of-band analog E-stops, STO circuits               |

: **Handoffs-by-limits synthesis grid**: A five-by-five matrix mapping five canonical signal handoffs ($\SignalHandoff_1\text{--}\SignalHandoff_5$) across the Boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), Brain (@sec-brain), Body (@sec-body), and Nervous System (@sec-nervous) against five physical limits ($\Latency, \Bandwidth, \HeatDissipationPower, \TimingJitter, \FaultDomainIsolation$). Cells marked *BINDING* are the budgets that drive selection; *Non-binding* means the scenario budget meets that dimension with margin. These illustrative allocations organize the timing and isolation evidence still required; a non-binding cell is not a qualification verdict. {#tbl-04-synthesis-grid tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

::: {#dfn-nervous-handoff-record .callout-definition title="Handoff record"}

***Handoff record***\index{Handoff record!definition} is the record that states one interface limit at one of the five handoffs between sensing and actuation: its value, the conditions under which it holds, its uncertainty and margin, the detector that catches an excursion, its provenance, and whether the value is a requirement, a proven bound, or a measured distribution.

1.  **Significance**: It is the second record in the record chain, after the limit record of the Body, and the first that ties a timing claim to the interface where the time is spent. On the running machine its $\SignalHandoff_4$ entry is the `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str` chunk lease, recorded as a requirement whose margin depends on the intervals of @tbl-04-event-timing.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a limit record, which describes a physical envelope of the plant such as credible deceleration, a handoff record describes an interface between two subsystems and names the clock on which its times are expressed. Unlike a latency in a profiling log, it states its bound kind, so a percentile cannot pass for a worst case.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Recording a bench $\text{p99}$ as a proven bound. The record then carries a number that the permission path trusts in conditions the bench never reached.

:::

Every boundary condition in the grid is recorded this way, so the budgets survive changes of hardware, firmware, and model. Each entry carries the six elements of a limit record and adds the fields that locate the limit at a handoff and state what evidence supports it (@tbl-04-schema-notebook).

| Field Name               | Physical SI Units                                                             | Structural Invariant & Description                                                                                                              |
|:-------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `signal_id`              | dimensionless                                                                 | Unique alphanumeric identifier (for example, `SIG_VIO_01`, `SIG_TRQ_AX1`).                                                                      |
| `source_subsystem`       | dimensionless                                                                 | Originating hardware or software module (`Camera_SerDes`, `Planner_VLA`).                                                                       |
| `destination_subsystem`  | dimensionless                                                                 | Receiving hardware or software module (`State_Estimator`, `Safety_MCU`).                                                                        |
| `handoff`                | dimensionless                                                                 | The handoff the signal crosses ($\SignalHandoff_1$ to $\SignalHandoff_5$).                                                                      |
| `physical_dimension`     | dimensionless                                                                 | Target limit category ($\Latency$, $\Bandwidth$, $\HeatDissipationPower$, $\TimingJitter$, $\FaultDomainIsolation$).                            |
| `value`                  | SI units ($\text{ms}$, $\text{MB/s}$, $\text{W}$, $\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}$) | Allocated budget, or the measured distribution it is checked against; for $\SignalHandoff_4$, the chunk lease derived from the stopping budget. |
| `conditions`             | as recorded                                                                   | Payload, temperature, supply voltage, firmware build, and concurrent workload under which the value holds; the value lapses when they change.   |
| `uncertainty`            | same as `value`                                                               | Error bound of the instrument or model that produced the value.                                                                                 |
| `margin`                 | same as `value`                                                               | Engineering margin between the operating target and the breakdown threshold.                                                                    |
| `detector`               | dimensionless                                                                 | Runtime monitor that catches an excursion (for example, a lease timer, a rail-voltage monitor, or a phase-current sensor).                      |
| `provenance`             | dimensionless                                                                 | Source of the value, including its evidence category (measured, derived, datasheet, or illustrative).                                           |
| `bound_kind`             | dimensionless                                                                 | `requirement`, `proven bound`, or `measured distribution`; only a proven bound may stand in for a worst case.                                   |
| `clock_domain`           | dimensionless                                                                 | Clock on which every time-valued field is expressed; a handoff that feeds the permission path uses the safety microcontroller's clock.          |
| `verification_timestamp` | UTC timestamp                                                                 | Date of bench falsification and sign-off; a log field, never an input to an age test.                                                           |

: **Conceptual fields of the handoff record**: The six limit-record elements of @sec-body-limit-record-schema, extended with the handoff, bound kind, and clock domain that locate a limit in the machine and state what evidence supports it. {#tbl-04-schema-notebook tbl-colwidths="[22,24,54]"}

The four timing events of @tbl-04-event-timing sit on this grid's handoffs, capture within $\SignalHandoff_1$, dispatch at $\SignalHandoff_2$, admission at $\SignalHandoff_4$, and brake onset at $\SignalHandoff_5$, so the grid's latency column follows the same single execution path as the timing table, and every time in it is expressed on the safety microcontroller's clock. Together, those rows show that the chunk lease at $\SignalHandoff_4$ cannot be chosen in isolation from the stopping distance below it or the inference renewal rate above it.

### Coupling the distance, lease, and supply budgets {#sec-nervous-coupled-budget}

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-coupled-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PART I COUPLED BUDGET: DISTANCE -> LEASE -> SUPPLY -> LEASE RULE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-coupled-budget.
# │ Goal:    Join Ch2's distance terms, this chapter's lease, and Ch3's supply
# │          rates into the lease rule for the running machine.
# │ Show:    ceiling 258.3 ms; running total 835.5 mm; intent sweep 98.0 ms,
# │          intent 2 Hz / 336 ms computed (INT4 sweep 24.5 ms); chunk sweep
# │          1.12 ms, 20 Hz / 40 ms;
# │          50 + 5 = 55 ms < 60 ms lease; upper limit 236.3 ms, 184.7 ms
# │          after the 51.6 ms capture-to-dispatch age, 121.4 ms after the
# │          114.9 ms capture-to-admission age of @tbl-04-event-timing
# │          (@eq-nervous-lease-rule).
# │ How:     ceiling and running total read from MachineLeaseBudget;
# │          calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization on RM / AISLE; the 5 ms renewal jitter is a scenario assumption.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PartOneCoupledBudget:
    """The chunk lease as the meeting point of Part I's distance, timing, and supply budgets."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    f_intent = RM.intent_rate  # category: chosen
    t_intent = RM.intent_inference_latency  # category: derived (prefill plus decode, @sec-brain-memory-wall)
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    t_chunk = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative (P99, incl. vision)
    t_renewal_jitter = MachineLeaseBudget.t_renewal_jitter  # category: chosen (from calc-nervous-machine-lease-budget)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_ceiling = MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling  # from calc-nervous-machine-lease-budget
    running_total = MachineLeaseBudget.running_total  # one source for the stopping budget

    intent_sweep = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=RM.intent_weight_memory,  # deployed INT4 weights
        memory_bandwidth=RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth,
        chunk_horizon=RM.chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=RM.dram_efficiency,
    )["t_stream"].to(millisecond)
    chunk_sweep = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=memory_from_params(RM.chunk_model.parameters, BYTES_FP16 / param),
        memory_bandwidth=RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth,
        chunk_horizon=RM.chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=RM.dram_efficiency,
    )["t_stream"].to(millisecond)

    t_chunk_period = (1 / f_chunk).to(millisecond)
    t_renewal_need = (t_chunk_period + t_renewal_jitter).to(millisecond)  # lease lower limit
    t_lease_upper = (t_ceiling - t_tick - t_bus - t_act).to(millisecond)  # before observation age
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # capture-to-dispatch age only (@sec-perception)
    t_lease_upper_age = (t_lease_upper - t_age).to(millisecond)  # before the dispatch-to-admission allocation
    t_age_admit = CaptureToBrakeTiming.t_replace  # capture to admission, rows 1 + 2 of @tbl-04-event-timing
    t_lease_upper_admit = (t_lease_upper - t_age_admit).to(millisecond)  # with Delta_da allocated
    mm_per_ms = (v * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_ceiling.magnitude - 258.333) < 5e-3, f"Pre-brake ceiling drifted: {t_ceiling}")
    check(abs(running_total.magnitude - 835.5) < 1e-6, f"Running total drifted: {running_total}")
    # 2026-09-28 (M2): deployed INT4 intent weights; ACT corrected to about 80M parameters.
    check(abs(intent_sweep.magnitude - 24.51) < 5e-3, f"Intent weight sweep drifted: {intent_sweep}")
    check(abs(chunk_sweep.magnitude - 1.1204) < 5e-4, f"Chunk weight sweep drifted: {chunk_sweep}")
    check(abs(f_chunk.to(hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk rate drifted: {f_chunk}")
    check(abs(f_intent.to(hertz).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Intent rate drifted: {f_intent}")
    check(abs(t_chunk.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk inference latency drifted: {t_chunk}")
    check(abs(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude - 335.61) < 5e-3, f"Intent inference latency drifted: {t_intent}")
    check(abs(t_chunk_period.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-6, f"Chunk period drifted: {t_chunk_period}")
    check(t_intent > t_lease, "The intent model must be unable to renew a chunk lease")
    check(t_chunk < t_chunk_period, "Chunk inference must finish within the chunk period")
    check(abs(t_renewal_need.magnitude - 55.0) < 1e-6, f"Lease lower limit drifted: {t_renewal_need}")
    check(t_renewal_need < t_lease, "Lease rule: chunk period plus jitter must be shorter than the lease")
    check(abs(t_lease_upper.magnitude - 236.333) < 5e-3, f"Lease upper limit (before age) drifted: {t_lease_upper}")
    check(t_lease <= t_lease_upper - AISLE.perception_age, "Lease rule: lease must fit the ceiling after tick, bus, onset, and age")
    check(abs(t_age.magnitude - 51.6) < 1e-6, f"Capture-to-dispatch age drifted: {t_age}")
    # margin_lease_rule_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 55, 60, and 121.4 ms.
    check(abs(t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Lease drifted: {t_lease}")
    check(abs(t_lease_upper_age.magnitude - 184.733) < 5e-3, f"Lease upper limit after age drifted: {t_lease_upper_age}")
    check(abs(t_lease_upper_admit.magnitude - 121.423) < 5e-3, f"Lease upper limit at admission drifted: {t_lease_upper_admit}")
    check(t_lease < t_lease_upper_admit, "Lease rule: the lease must still fit once Delta_da is allocated")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    t_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(t_ceiling, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    running_total_str = fmt_length(running_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    intent_sweep_str = fmt_latency(intent_sweep, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_intent_str = fmt_latency(round(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_intent_str = fmt_frequency(f_intent, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    chunk_sweep_str = fmt_latency(chunk_sweep, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    f_chunk_str = fmt_frequency(f_chunk, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_jitter_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_jitter, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_need_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_need, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_upper_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_upper, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_lease_upper_age_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_upper_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_admit_str = fmt_latency(t_age_admit, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_lease_upper_admit_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_upper_admit, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    mm_per_ms_str = fmt_length(mm_per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

Shortening the chunk lease to save stopping distance without checking how fast the proposer renews causes the lease to expire before the next chunk arrives so the robot stutters from stop to stop, whereas lengthening the lease to ride out slow renewals lets the robot overrun its rack-end clearance before braking begins. The machine's physical, cognitive, and nervous subsystems therefore meet at a single shared budget, with the chunk lease at their point of convergence. In @sec-body-kinetic-momentum, the loaded machine moving at its `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.v_str` drive limit had to come to a complete stop within the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.d_clear_str` clearance available at a rack end, and accounting for deceleration mechanics and fixed braking overheads left `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_ceiling_str` for all computational and communication activities preceding brake onset. @Sec-nervous-lease-sizing then allocated a portion of this window: when a proposer stalls, it retains motion authority for one chunk lease before the emergency stop command reaches the motor drives one tick and one bus cycle later, bringing the running stopping budget to `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.running_total_str`.

Because the proposer needs enough time to renew that lease before it expires, @sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline sets the lower bound from what each learned model can supply. The intent model's INT4 weights require `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.intent_sweep_str` just to stream across the memory bus, and a complete inference pass of compute-bound prefill followed by bandwidth-bound autoregressive decoding consumes `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_intent_str`, which means that at `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.f_intent_str` the intent model cannot renew proposals on tens-of-milliseconds timescales. By contrast, the action chunking policy streams its parameters in `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.chunk_sweep_str`, and its target `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.f_chunk_str` cadence supplies a fresh trajectory chunk every `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_chunk_period_str`. Its illustrative `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_chunk_str` $\text{p99}$ inference latency makes this cadence a feasible nominal supply target rather than a guaranteed worst-case bound, so intercepting late, dropped, or corrupt renewals remains the responsibility of the independent permission path.

::: {.column-margin}
<!-- fig-alt hand-types 55, 60, and 121.4 ms; PartOneCoupledBudget guards them.
     Drawn by generate_margin_figures.py (ch04_lease_rule_envelope); --check fails on drift. -->
![](images/svg/margin_lease_rule_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars in milliseconds against a dashed red upper limit at 121.4 milliseconds, the lease limit after the full capture-to-admission age: renewal floor 55 milliseconds and lease 60 milliseconds, both far to the left of the ceiling."}

*The lease must outlast renewal and expire well before the stopping budget runs out.*
:::

These constraints dictate the **lease rule**\index{Chunk lease!lease rule} for the machine. For continuous, uninterrupted trajectory tracking, the lease duration must exceed the proposer's renewal interval plus an allowance for tail jitter. Simultaneously, to guarantee physical safety, the lease must fit within the pre-brake ceiling of @eq-nervous-prebrake once detection latency, bus transport, actuator brake onset, and sensor evidence age at admission are deducted:
$$\ChunkRenewalPeriod + \RenewalJitterAllowance < \ChunkLease \le \frac{\ClearDistance - \LocalizationBound - \ProtectiveClearanceMargin - \SpeedAtDetection^2/2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration}{\SpeedAtDetection} - \PermissionLoopPeriod - \CommandTransportTime - \ActuatorResponseTime - \ObservationAge$$ {#eq-nervous-lease-rule}
where $\ChunkRenewalPeriod$ is the chunk policy's nominal renewal period, $\RenewalJitterAllowance$ is the margin allocated for interarrival timing variations, and $\ObservationAge$ is charged as the evidence's age at admission, rows 1 and 2 of @tbl-04-event-timing together, not its age at dispatch alone. This inequality captures the coupled cyber-physical budget in a single mathematical relation. The left side reflects compute supply, bounded by the neural proposer. The first term on the right reflects physical mechanics, governed by vehicle speed, workspace clearance, and braking deceleration. The remaining subtractive terms account for detection and communication delays, actuator brake onset, and the observation age accumulated across the perception pipeline. A faster vehicle, a less aggressive brake, or a tighter workspace lowers the upper bound; a slower or more jitter-prone neural network raises the lower bound. If the two bounds cross, no lease can preserve both uninterrupted proposal tracking and the stopping guarantee at that velocity; the permission path must interrupt tracking before authority expires.

On the mobile manipulator, the lower bound evaluates to the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_renewal_need_str` renewal floor derived in notebook \ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}. The upper bound provides `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_upper_str` prior to deducting observation age; subtracting the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_age_str` capture-to-dispatch age allocated in row 1 of @tbl-04-event-timing leaves `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_upper_age_str`. Because the observation must also traverse the dispatch-to-admission pipeline before execution, charging that interval's budget from @tbl-04-event-timing increases total evidence age at admission to `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_age_admit_str`, leaving an effective upper limit of `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_upper_admit_str`. This is the same subtraction as the notebook's, taken in a different order. The notebook charged the lease first and left `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling_left_str` under the ceiling for evidence age and the stop profile; the lease rule charges the age first and leaves this limit for the lease. The selected `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_str` lease sits just above the lower renewal bound, reflecting the physical reality that every additional millisecond of lease duration consumes `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.mm_per_ms_str` of stopping clearance at maximum drive velocity. This value remains an unverified allocation until the physical vehicle demonstrates that all constituent intervals fit within budget under load. Artificially inflating the lease duration to mask software latency spikes merely consumes stopping clearance, trading mechanical safety margin for compute slack.

Because each chunk packages base velocities and arm joint targets together, the architecture enforces a single shared chunk lease across both subsystems. When that lease expires, each physical body must execute a kinematically feasible, state-matched fallback maneuver. The base's `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_ceiling_str` pre-brake ceiling governs this allocation; it does not imply that the arm possesses surplus margin. The arm analysis in @sec-planning-handoff evaluates stopping distance and response travel against its own localized workspace clearances. Validating the shared lease requires verifying timing, evidence age, dynamic state, and fallback limits simultaneously across both base and manipulator. The goal the intent model supplies is governed by a different timer, the intent lease, which limits how long a high-level goal remains active before it must be renewed and is sized in its own chapter, not from this stopping budget.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The intent lease and its contract are developed in @sec-intent-lease.
:::

::: {#chk-nervous-handoffs-grid .callout-checkpoint title="The handoffs matrix and physical budgets"}

Before testing the lease on a humanoid and reviewing the engineering fallacies, verify your understanding of system-wide interface contracts:

- [ ] **Binding physical constraints**: Can you explain why sensory handoffs bind first on bandwidth and exposure latency, whereas actuation handoffs bind first on determinism and heat?
- [ ] **Handoff record provenance**: Can you describe why every numerical limit in an autonomous system must record its evidence category, operating conditions, bound kind, and verification status?
- [ ] **The lease rule**: Can you state the two limits on the chunk lease, one set by successful-admission interarrival and one by the pre-brake ceiling, and explain why a p99 inference time alone proves neither?
